Anthropic must scale systems, controls, reporting and hiring while keeping its culture, and it increasingly relies on outside chip, data center and software providers that must grow with it. Buying too much or too little compute could raise costs or limit service. Poorly managed growth could weaken controls and compliance, draw regulators' attention, and harm products, customers and the brand.

paras.p414: Anthropic has lost money every year, including $42.0B in 2025 and $80.7B in the first half of 2026; most of that ($34.3B and $72.4B) reflects its rising valuation increasing what its convertible notes are worth.
paras.p415: Anthropic says it has spent heavily to grow and will keep doing so, in the following areas.
paras.p416: The first area is securing compute, meaning the specialized chips in data centers that train and run Claude.
paras.p417: Anthropic keeps spending on research to stay at the leading edge of AI models and to add new features to its products.
paras.p418: Anthropic is expanding its sales and marketing efforts.
paras.p420: Anthropic is expanding its operations in multiple countries and regions.
paras.p421: Anthropic is growing its administrative functions, such as finance, legal and human resources.
paras.p422: Anthropic must pay to comply with current and changing rules on AI, data protection, privacy and security.
paras.p423: Anthropic spends on AI safety work, including testing, monitoring and reducing risks from its models.
paras.p424: Being a public company brings extra costs, such as reporting and compliance.
paras.p425: Anthropic also bears the cost of lawsuits and other legal proceedings.
paras.p426: Anthropic has signed purchase and lease commitments, as of and after September 30, 2026, whose total is left blank in this draft; these could raise costs sharply and may not produce matching revenue growth.
paras.p427: Employee stock grants (RSUs) become an expense when the IPO happens; measured at June 30, 2026, that means $2.9B at once and $23.7B over about 2.1 years, plus $3.1B for other awards and more for new grants.
paras.p428: If revenue does not grow faster than rising costs, Anthropic may keep losing large amounts of money and may never become consistently profitable.

s63.tldr: Anthropic has lost money every year: $42.0B in 2025 and $80.7B in the first half of 2026, mostly ($34.3B and $72.4B) because its rising valuation increased what its convertible notes are worth. It will keep spending on compute (chips that train and run Claude), research, sales, staff, expansion abroad, administration, compliance, AI safety, public company costs and lawsuits. Purchase and lease commitments (total not yet stated) could sharply raise costs without matching revenue. Employee stock grants become an expense at the IPO: measured at June 30, 2026, $2.9B at once and $23.7B over about 2.1 years, plus $3.1B for other awards. Unless revenue outpaces costs, Anthropic may never be consistently profitable.

paras.p429: Anthropic's results swing from period to period, partly because large, irregular spending on research, compute, and expansion can raise losses or cut margins even when the underlying business is improving.
paras.p430: Some revenue comes from customers later found breaking Anthropic's usage rules; enforcement, stepped up in August and September 2026, is expected to reduce that share and may lower overall revenue and growth.
paras.p431: Because customers pay by usage, revenue already dips around summer and winter holidays and moves with model release timing; rapid growth has hidden these patterns, which Anthropic expects to become more visible.
paras.p432: This introduces a list of further, often uncontrollable, factors that can make results swing.
paras.p433: Demand for Anthropic's products, and how well Anthropic forecasts it.
paras.p434: Whether Anthropic can forecast and obtain the compute it needs, and what it costs.
paras.p435: Whether Anthropic can spread use of its products within customer organizations.
paras.p436: Whether Anthropic can win and keep customers and sell more to existing ones.
paras.p437: How well Anthropic manages the outside providers it depends on for critical infrastructure.
paras.p438: The timing and success of new features from Anthropic and from competitors.
paras.p439: Delays from Anthropic's safety measures or from laws governing when advanced AI models can be released.
paras.p440: Whether Anthropic's products achieve broad acceptance and use.
paras.p441: New competitors and products entering the market.
paras.p442: Security breaches, technical problems, or service interruptions.
paras.p443: Actual or perceived misuse or leaks of confidential or personal data.
paras.p444: Pressure to lower prices from competition or other causes.
paras.p445: Losing lawsuits, paying settlements, or other legal costs.
paras.p447: When stock awards are granted or vest for employees, directors, or consultants.
paras.p448: Settling restricted stock units (shares promised to employees), including cash Anthropic pays for employees' taxes and the related accounting expense.
paras.p449: Whether Anthropic can protect and strengthen its brand.
paras.p450: Foreign currencies losing value against the U.S. dollar.
paras.p451: Changing and uncertain laws and regulation for the AI industry.
paras.p452: Government investigations, fines, orders, or settlements.
paras.p453: Rising compliance costs in current and new markets.
paras.p454: Costs of acquiring companies, talent, or technology, including possible write downs.
paras.p455: Disasters that interrupt the availability of Anthropic's products.
paras.p456: Economic and geopolitical conditions in the U.S. and abroad that affect software spending.
paras.p457: Any of these factors could push results below Anthropic's guidance or analysts' expectations, which could lower the price of its Class A stock.

s64.tldr: Anthropic's results can swing sharply from period to period. One reason is large, irregular spending on research, compute (the specialized chips in data centers that train and run Claude) and expansion, which can deepen losses even when the business improves. Anthropic stepped up enforcement against customers breaking its usage rules in August and September 2026, which may lower revenue and growth. Usage-based billing already causes dips around summer and winter holidays and shifts with model releases, patterns that rapid growth has hidden. Other causes include demand and compute forecasting, competition and price pressure, outages and breaches, legal and regulatory costs, employee stock award timing and related tax payments, currency moves and acquisitions. Missing guidance or analyst expectations could lower the Class A stock price.

paras.p458: Metrics such as Run Rate Revenue, Net Revenue Retention, customer counts, and Claude's success rate come from Anthropic's own systems, are not independently checked, and may not reflect actual or future results.
paras.p459: Run Rate Revenue projects a short recent window over a full year, so it swings with seasons, includes rule breaking customers not yet cut off, and is not actual revenue or a forecast.
paras.p460: Anthropic does not track enterprise customers as a category; it treats customers paying $100,000 or more over the trailing twelve months as enterprises, a judgment based count that may overstate or understate real enterprise adoption.
paras.p461: Claude's success rates come from tests Anthropic designed itself, so customers may get different results and the figures may not be comparable to those reported by other AI developers.
paras.p462: Anthropic's metrics depend partly on partner data and imperfect internal tools, may be recalculated over time, and may differ from other companies' similarly named measures, so investors should not rely heavily on them.

s65.tldr: Anthropic's key metrics, such as Run Rate Revenue, Net Revenue Retention, customer counts and Claude's success rate, come from its own systems, partner data and imperfect tools. They are not independently checked, may be recalculated, and may differ from other companies' similarly named measures. Run Rate Revenue scales a short recent window up to a full year, so it swings with seasons, includes rule-breaking customers not yet cut off, and is neither actual revenue nor a forecast. Anthropic counts customers paying $100,000 or more over the trailing twelve months as enterprises, a judgment that may misstate real enterprise adoption. Success rates come from Anthropic's own tests, so customers' results may differ.

paras.p463: Governments in the US, the EU and elsewhere are writing AI rules quickly and inconsistently, from the EU AI Act in force since August 2024 to state safety laws and a June 2026 federal executive order, and proposals as drastic as nationalization could constrain Anthropic.
paras.p464: Anthropic itself lobbies for oversight of frontier AI, meaning the most advanced models, so that safety keeps pace with capability, but those rules would bind Anthropic too, could slow its growth, and its advocacy has already drawn criticism.
paras.p465: Public worry about AI replacing jobs or harming the environment could push governments to slow or tax AI adoption, and Anthropic might voluntarily spend money to soften job losses without getting any business return or guaranteed effect.
paras.p466: Tighter rules in the US and Europe could let less regulated rivals move faster, and US and China rivalry could produce restrictions on dealing with Chinese markets and Chinese retaliation against American AI products.
paras.p467: This introduces a list of specific kinds of regulatory limits Anthropic could face.
paras.p468: Governments could forbid or attach conditions to particular uses of AI.
paras.p469: Anthropic could be forced to change, delay or pull models in some markets, and in early 2026 the Department of War already suggested using the Defense Production Act to make it drop its limits on autonomous weapons and mass surveillance.
paras.p470: Rules could require more disclosure, record keeping, audits and human supervision of AI systems.
paras.p471: Privacy, intellectual property or other laws could restrict what data Anthropic can collect, move or keep to train and run its models.
paras.p472: Regulators or courts could require outside approval before new models are built or released, and in September 2026 a state attorney general already asked a court to impose such a requirement on an AI company.
paras.p473: Permitting, zoning, or limits on power and water use could block or slow the data centers Anthropic needs.
paras.p474: Stricter energy efficiency and environmental rules could add cost.
paras.p475: Export controls could stop Anthropic selling in some countries, and in June 2026 the Commerce Department already restricted Fable 5 and Mythos 5 worldwide until Anthropic strengthened its safeguards, so this has happened and could recur.
paras.p476: Governments could impose AI-specific taxes, fees or reporting duties.
paras.p477: At the extreme, activities central to Anthropic or its customers could be banned outright or paused.
paras.p478: Because rules differ by place and keep changing, Anthropic cannot predict them, may need costly compliance work or have to pull back from some markets, and rules hitting its customers could also shrink demand.
paras.p479: Debates over whether AI could be conscious or deserve moral consideration could bring rules or pressure on how Anthropic builds models, and Anthropic may adopt its own self-imposed limits that raise costs or reduce commercial potential.

s66.tldr: AI rules are arriving fast and inconsistently, including the EU AI Act and a June 2026 federal executive order, and some have already hit Anthropic. In June 2026 the Commerce Department restricted Fable 5 and Mythos 5 worldwide until Anthropic strengthened its safeguards. In early 2026 the Department of War floated using the Defense Production Act to force it to drop its limits on autonomous weapons and mass surveillance. Other threats include bans on certain uses, outside approval before releases (a state attorney general sought this against an AI company in September 2026), data limits, data center permitting, AI taxes and even nationalization. Anthropic's own push for oversight binds it too, and job loss fears, US China rivalry and debates over AI consciousness add pressure.

paras.p480: Government agencies account for only about 1% of Anthropic's revenue in each period shown, but government actions can also affect its commercial customers and partners, and the list that follows sets out the extra risks of selling to governments.
paras.p481: Government budget or purchasing policy changes could cut spending on Anthropic's contracts.
paras.p482: Government programs or their requirements could change.
paras.p483: Anthropic may fail to agree terms with governments, including on what its models may be used for.
paras.p484: Its employees might not receive the security clearances needed for government work.
paras.p485: It must keep facility clearances, meaning government approval of its premises, to work on classified contracts.
paras.p486: A change of administration could shift priorities and funding.
paras.p487: The government's view of Anthropic or its technology could turn against it.
paras.p488: Losing bidders could protest contract awards, and procurement disputes could lead to litigation.
paras.p489: New or changed laws could affect government sales.
paras.p490: Budget cuts, stopgap funding and government shutdowns could disrupt contracts and payments.
paras.p491: Third parties could compete for or influence government contracts.
paras.p492: Shifting security or privacy laws and attitudes could affect government business.
paras.p493: Wars, terrorism, disasters or health crises could delay government funding and purchasing.
paras.p494: Other outside factors could add cost or delay.
paras.p495: Any of these could lead governments to cancel, shrink or avoid contracts with Anthropic, and could damage its ties with partners and customers that themselves sell to governments.
paras.p496: In February 2026 the President ordered agencies to stop using Anthropic and the Department of War labeled it a supply-chain risk after Anthropic refused mass surveillance and autonomous weapons uses; Anthropic largely won in district court on August 27, 2026, but lost a 2-1 appeals ruling on September 25, 2026, and is seeking full-court review.
paras.p497: When the Commerce Department restricted Fable 5 and Mythos 5 worldwide in June 2026, Anthropic had to switch them off for every customer until the restrictions were lifted, and that could happen again.
paras.p498: Even apart from how the lawsuits end, these fights could hurt Anthropic's reputation, make customers hesitate or demand exit rights, deter long-term partnerships, and make demand and investor sentiment more volatile.
paras.p499: Winning government contracts is slow and costly with no guaranteed payoff, and because contracts often come in optional phases, the revenue actually earned can fall short of the headline contract value.
paras.p500: Government contracts carry special rules, such as the right to cancel at any time for convenience, which can leave Anthropic with less revenue than expected.
paras.p501: Anthropic's subsidiary Anthropic Public Institutions, LLC must keep a security clearance to do classified federal work, and losing it would block new classified contracts and could end existing ones.
paras.p502: Government audits or rule breaches could bring contract cancellations, fines, loss of eligibility for future government sales, or even criminal liability.

s67.tldr: Government agencies bring only about 1% of Anthropic's revenue, but government actions have already hurt it. After Anthropic refused mass surveillance and autonomous weapons uses, the President in February 2026 ordered agencies to stop using it, and the Department of War labeled it a supply-chain risk. Anthropic largely won in district court on August 27, 2026, lost a 2-1 appeal on September 25, 2026, and is seeking full-court review. The June 2026 Commerce restrictions forced it to switch off Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for all customers. Such fights could deter customers and partners. Government contracts are slow to win, can be canceled at will, and often bring in less than their headline value. Losing a subsidiary's security clearance would block classified work, and violations could bring fines or criminal liability.

paras.p503: Anthropic depends on three cloud providers, Amazon, Google and Microsoft, plus suppliers such as Broadcom, for its compute, and outages, worse renewal terms or a forced switch to other providers would be costly and could reduce efficiency.
paras.p504: Amazon, Google and Microsoft are at once Anthropic's investors, suppliers, customers, sales channels and competitors with their own AI models, which gives them insight into its pricing and reasons to favor their own products.
paras.p505: These overlapping roles create conflicts of interest: the cloud providers or Broadcom could favor their own needs or rival customers, change terms, or limit Anthropic's compute, and the ties have drawn and could draw antitrust scrutiny.
paras.p506: This closes the section by saying failure to manage these partner risks could harm Anthropic's results.

s68.tldr: Anthropic depends on three cloud providers, Amazon, Google and Microsoft, and on suppliers such as Broadcom for compute, the specialized chips in data centers that train and run Claude. Outages, worse renewal terms or a forced switch to other providers would be costly. The three cloud providers are also Anthropic's investors, customers, sales channels and competitors with their own AI models. That gives them insight into its pricing and reasons to favor themselves or rival customers, change terms or limit its compute. These overlapping ties have drawn, and could draw more, antitrust scrutiny.

paras.p507: To rely less on cloud providers, Anthropic is building its own data center capacity, including the 2026 Lease Arrangement with about $125.2B of equipment rent over five years that cannot be canceled, with cash already set aside for Broadcom in April 2026, despite limited experience running such projects.
paras.p508: As Anthropic buys pieces of compute separately from many companies, it may have to pay each one when its part is done even if another party's delay leaves the equipment unusable, risking large cash outflows without working capacity.
paras.p509: Some setups chain together chip suppliers, financing firms, facility developers and operators, so a failure by any one of them can hold up the whole system.
paras.p510: Anthropic has also taken on power plants and other energy assets to feed its data centers, bringing new regulatory and environmental liabilities and the challenge of finishing power and data center projects on matching schedules.
paras.p511: These projects can be delayed or run over budget for many reasons, some depend on credit support from a competitor, construction guarantees may lapse if a lender forecloses, and new tariffs can be passed on to Anthropic.
paras.p512: Unlike flexible cloud rentals, owned and leased infrastructure locks Anthropic into payments even if needs or technology change, with some power and data center deals running 20 years with rising rents, take-or-pay terms where it pays whether or not it uses the capacity, and uncapped fuel costs.
paras.p513: Building its own infrastructure shifts Anthropic toward large payments made well before capacity comes online, so it expects heavy cash outflows for the foreseeable future that may grow even if results improve, and may need to raise money on worse terms.
paras.p514: If the data center effort is late, over budget or mismatched to its needs, Anthropic may not get the expected benefits and its finances could suffer.

s69.tldr: Anthropic is building its own data center capacity despite limited experience. This includes the 2026 Lease Arrangement, about $125.2B of equipment rent over five years that cannot be canceled, with cash already set aside for Broadcom in April 2026. Because it buys parts from many firms, it may have to pay each one even if another's delay leaves equipment unusable, and one failure in a chain of suppliers, financiers, developers and operators can stall everything. Its power plants add environmental and regulatory liabilities. Some deals run 20 years with rising rents, uncapped fuel costs and take-or-pay terms, meaning it pays even for unused capacity. Some also rely on a competitor's credit support. Heavy upfront cash outflows are expected for the foreseeable future, possibly requiring costly fundraising.

paras.p515: Anthropic is building a larger direct sales team but has limited experience doing so, faces stiff competition to hire salespeople who understand complex AI products, and finds this hardest when expanding outside the U.S.
paras.p516: Reorganizing the sales team or changing how salespeople are paid can temporarily hurt productivity, and if new hires do not start selling effectively soon enough, revenue could grow more slowly or fall.

s70.tldr: Anthropic is building a larger direct sales team with limited experience doing so. It competes hard to hire salespeople who understand complex AI products, and this is hardest outside the U.S. Reorganizing the team or changing how salespeople are paid can temporarily hurt productivity. If new hires do not start selling effectively soon enough, revenue could grow more slowly or fall.

paras.p517: Anthropic has only a short track record selling usage-based access and subscriptions under its current model, so its business approach is not fully proven and its future results are hard to forecast.
paras.p518: Claude has spread mostly through individual developers and power users who then bring it into their employers, so if bigger consumer-focused rivals win those individuals first, Anthropic's small sales team may not make up the lost business.

s71.tldr: Anthropic has only a short track record selling usage-based access and subscriptions under its current model, so its approach is not fully proven and its results are hard to forecast. Claude has spread mainly through individual developers and power users who bring it into their workplaces. If larger, consumer-focused rivals win those people first, Anthropic's small sales team may not recover the lost business.

paras.p519: Large businesses provide much of Anthropic's revenue and demand strong reliability, security and detailed records of what autonomous AI agents do, and they may hesitate to give tools like Claude Code and Claude Cowork the deep system access they need.
paras.p520: Selling to large businesses is slow and expensive, requiring custom work, extra features and support before any purchase, and many buy through cloud providers' marketplaces such as Amazon, Google or Microsoft, which adds rules outside Anthropic's control.
paras.p521: Education needs, budget cycles, approvals, procurement and legal review make the time from first contact to signed deal vary widely, and large business deals take longer than sales to individuals or small firms.
paras.p522: A meaningful share of revenue comes from a fairly small number of large customers, so one of them cutting spending sharply could noticeably change Anthropic's results in a given quarter.
paras.p523: Large businesses that already work closely with competitors may delay or reject a switch to Anthropic.
paras.p524: Large customers are especially sensitive to downtime, and keeping service fast and available for them uses more of Anthropic's limited computing capacity, the specialized chips in data centers that run Claude, which could squeeze other uses.
paras.p525: Winning large business customers depends on building an effective sales organization, linking this risk back to the earlier one about hiring and keeping salespeople.

s72.tldr: Large businesses supply much of Anthropic's revenue, and a fairly small number of them account for a meaningful share, so one cutting spending sharply could noticeably move a quarter's results. These customers demand strong reliability, security and records of what autonomous AI agents do, and may hesitate to give Claude Code and Claude Cowork deep access to their systems. Selling to them is slow, costly and unpredictable, needing custom work and support. Many buy through marketplaces run by Amazon, Google or Microsoft, whose rules Anthropic does not control. Firms tied to competitors may resist switching. Serving customers who cannot tolerate downtime uses scarce compute, the chips that run Claude. Success depends on building an effective sales team.

paras.p526: Anthropic offers free versions to build awareness and reach individual workers, but free users cost money in computing and support, may never pay, may replace would-be paying customers, and their value is hard to measure.

s73.tldr: Anthropic offers free versions to build awareness and reach individual workers, but free users cost money in computing and support, may never pay, may replace would-be paying customers, and their value is hard to measure.

paras.p527: Customers depend on Anthropic's support teams for setup, troubleshooting, training and security help, and weak support, especially for large businesses with complex systems, could reduce renewals and expansion.
paras.p528: Anthropic's growth relies heavily on existing customers using Claude for more tasks, so if support cannot help them find valuable new uses and show a return, they may cut back or renew for less.
paras.p529: If sales grow faster than expected, Anthropic may not hire and train enough support staff in time, which would hurt service quality and customer satisfaction.
paras.p530: Serving a growing global customer base means offering support, training and documentation in other languages and across more time zones, which adds difficulty.

s74.tldr: Customers rely on Anthropic's support teams for setup, troubleshooting, training and security help. Weak support, especially for large businesses with complex systems, could reduce renewals and expansion. Because growth depends heavily on existing customers using Claude for more tasks, support must help them find valuable new uses and show a return. If sales grow faster than Anthropic can hire and train support staff, service could suffer. Serving a global customer base also adds the burden of other languages and more time zones.

paras.p531: Anthropic's safety commitments and its status as a public benefit corporation, a company legally required to weigh a public mission alongside profit, lead it to accept lower short-term revenue, and it has already delayed or limited releases, such as Mythos through Project Glasswing.
paras.p532: Safety work adds research, staff and infrastructure costs and can mean giving up revenue to competitors that release faster or with fewer restrictions, which may make Anthropic's products less attractive to some customers.
paras.p533: Anthropic may make pricing or access choices that earn less now than rivals do, investors and customers may see this as weakness, and Anthropic cannot promise the long-term payoff will arrive on time or at all.

s75.tldr: Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, a company legally required to weigh a public mission alongside profit. Its safety commitments and this status lead it to accept lower short-term revenue, and it has already delayed or limited releases, such as Mythos through Project Glasswing. Safety work adds research, staff and infrastructure costs and can hand revenue to rivals that release faster or with fewer limits, making its products less attractive to some customers. Pricing or access choices that earn less now may look like weakness to investors and customers, and the long-term payoff may come late or not at all.

paras.p534: New products and business lines require large upfront spending with uncertain results, and moving resources away from core products to fund them could slow existing growth if they fail.
paras.p535: Anthropic's life sciences lab work and robotics research take it beyond software into handling chemicals and biological materials, bringing new injury, contamination and regulatory risks, and any drug discoveries would face long, costly approval paths.

s76.tldr: New products and business lines need large upfront spending with uncertain results, and moving resources away from core products could slow existing growth if the new efforts fail. Life sciences lab work and robotics research take Anthropic beyond software into handling chemicals and biological materials. That adds injury, contamination and regulatory risks, and any drug discoveries would face long, costly approval.

paras.p536: Software updates and new model launches have already caused outages, including a March 2026 outage and slowdowns driven by a rapid jump in demand and computing shortages, and Anthropic says similar incidents may recur despite its fixes.
paras.p537: Because Anthropic buys computing capacity far ahead based on forecasts, a sudden rise in demand could leave it short, causing slowdowns or access limits for customers while also squeezing capacity for building new models.
paras.p538: Amazon, Google and Microsoft supply much of the computing infrastructure that runs Claude and Anthropic's internal tools, so problems or poor service at any of them would directly hurt Anthropic's customers and reputation.
paras.p539: Moving off Amazon, Google or Microsoft to another cloud provider would be slow and costly, and any of them raising prices, ending the relationship, or favoring competitors could harm Anthropic's finances.
paras.p540: A growing share of Anthropic's computing sits in leased data centers run by outside operators, some fairly new and with less backup than large clouds, and all facilities depend on reliable power and water supplies.

s77.tldr: Software updates and model launches have already caused outages, including a March 2026 outage and slowdowns from a rapid jump in demand and computing shortages, and similar incidents may recur. Anthropic buys computing capacity far ahead based on forecasts, so a sudden rise in demand could force slowdowns or access limits while squeezing capacity for building new models. Amazon, Google and Microsoft run much of Claude's infrastructure, so their problems hit Anthropic directly. Switching away from them would be slow and costly, and price increases, termination or favoring rivals could hurt its finances. A growing share of its computing sits in leased data centers run by outside operators, some new and with less backup, and all depend on reliable power and water.

paras.p541: Anthropic plans to keep buying companies and investing in others, including in young markets, but acquisitions may not integrate well or earn much, and it could overpay.
paras.p542: Competition from other buyers, high prices and antitrust rules could stop Anthropic from completing deals or force it to sell businesses, which could limit its ability to gain scale and technology.
paras.p543: This introduces a list of specific risks that acquisitions carry.
paras.p544: Competition for good targets can push up prices and make deals harder to complete on acceptable terms.
paras.p545: A deal may fail to close or be significantly delayed.
paras.p546: Deals can lead to lawsuits or legal claims.
paras.p547: Combining an acquired company's technology, operations, contracts and staff can be difficult.
paras.p548: Key employees, partners or customers of an acquired company may leave.
paras.p549: Merging an acquired company's brand with Anthropic's own can be challenging.
paras.p550: Deals can pull money and management attention away from existing operations or other opportunities.
paras.p551: Expected benefits and cost savings from a deal may not arrive at all or on schedule.
paras.p552: Deals may require borrowing or issuing new shares, which reduces existing shareholders' ownership percentage.
paras.p553: Anthropic may miss hidden problems at an acquired company, such as copyright, legal, compliance, accounting or employee issues.
paras.p554: An acquired company could harm Anthropic's internal culture.
paras.p555: New laws or regulations could hurt an acquired business after the deal.
paras.p556: Regulators may block or delay Anthropic's acquisitions.
paras.p557: Confidential information shared with possible acquisition targets could be stolen.
paras.p558: An acquired company or new service could take sales away from Anthropic's existing products.
paras.p559: The stock market could react badly to an acquisition.
paras.p560: If Anthropic fails to manage these acquisition and investment risks or does not get the expected benefits, its business and finances could suffer.

s78.tldr: Anthropic plans to keep buying and investing in companies, including in young markets, but deals may integrate poorly, earn little or be overpriced. Rival buyers, high prices, antitrust rules and regulators could block or delay deals or force Anthropic to sell businesses. Other risks include losing an acquired firm's key staff or customers, missing hidden copyright, legal or accounting problems, damage to culture, diverted cash and management attention, and lawsuits. Confidential information shared with targets could be stolen, new businesses could take sales from existing products, and the market could react badly. Borrowing or issuing new shares to pay for deals would reduce existing shareholders' ownership percentage.

paras.p561: Anthropic already draws heavy media attention, including stories about AI replacing jobs, misuse and catastrophic risks, and is often singled out even when concerns are not about its products, which could reduce demand and damage its brand.

s79.tldr: Anthropic already draws heavy media attention, including stories about AI replacing jobs, misuse and catastrophic risks, and is often singled out even when concerns are not about its products, which could reduce demand and damage its brand.

paras.p562: Becoming a public company listed on the Nasdaq Global Select Market brings new reporting rules and higher legal, accounting and insurance costs, which may also make it harder to recruit directors and executives.
paras.p563: Anthropic expects significant spending and new accounting hires to meet outside audit requirements for its financial controls under Sarbanes-Oxley Section 404, and it may face costly pressure from activist shareholders.
paras.p564: The detailed public disclosures required of a public company may invite lawsuits from competitors and others, which could cost money and distract leadership even if Anthropic wins.
paras.p565: Many of Anthropic's managers have little experience running a public company, so the new reporting duties and investor scrutiny could pull their attention away from running the business.

s80.tldr: Listing on the Nasdaq Global Select Market brings new reporting rules and higher legal, accounting and insurance costs, and may make recruiting directors and executives harder. Anthropic expects significant spending and new accounting hires to pass outside audits of its financial controls under Sarbanes-Oxley Section 404, and it may face costly pressure from activist shareholders. The detailed disclosures public companies must make may invite lawsuits from competitors and others. Many of its managers have little public company experience, so these duties could distract them from running the business.

paras.p566: War, terrorism, natural disasters, pandemics or power outages could damage or cut off the data centers, power, cooling and networks Anthropic relies on, its San Francisco Bay Area headquarters faces earthquake and fire risk, and its disaster plans and insurance may fall short.

s81.tldr: War, terrorism, natural disasters, pandemics or power outages could damage or cut off the data centers, power, cooling and networks Anthropic relies on, its San Francisco Bay Area headquarters faces earthquake and fire risk, and its disaster plans and insurance may fall short.

paras.p567: Claude has to connect with other companies' software through APIs, the interfaces programs use to talk to each other, and Anthropic depends on those companies, including competitors, granting access on terms they can change at will; the list below describes how.
paras.p568: One threat is that a software provider cuts off or restricts Anthropic's access to its software or interfaces.
paras.p569: Another is that a provider changes its rules or raises fees for Anthropic or other developers.
paras.p570: A provider could also change how Anthropic or its customers are able to reach information.
paras.p571: A provider could give better deals to one of Anthropic's competitors.
paras.p572: A provider could favor its own competing AI products over Anthropic's.
paras.p573: Downloads of the Claude app depend on Apple's App Store and Google's Play Store, so changes to their rules, fees, content policies, search rankings or device support could slow Anthropic's user growth or favor rival apps.
paras.p574: Other companies' products keep changing and Anthropic may not keep up, and competitors could deliberately alter their products or standards so Claude works worse with them, weakening Anthropic's position.

s82.tldr: Claude must connect with other companies' software through APIs, the interfaces programs use to talk to each other. Those companies, including competitors, can cut off access, change rules, raise fees, alter how data can be reached, or favor rivals or their own AI products. Downloads of the Claude app depend on Apple's App Store and Google's Play Store, whose rules, fees, rankings or device support could slow user growth or favor rival apps. Anthropic may also fail to keep up as other products change, and competitors could deliberately make their software work worse with Claude.

paras.p575: Anthropic's risks feed on each other: copyright losses could force model retraining, compute shortages could slow growth, and weak revenue could cause a default under its A&R Credit Agreement, its main loan agreement, triggering defaults and faster repayment elsewhere.

s83.tldr: Anthropic's risks feed on each other: copyright losses could force model retraining, compute shortages could slow growth, and weak revenue could cause a default under its A&R Credit Agreement, its main loan agreement, triggering defaults and faster repayment elsewhere.

s84.tldr: Anthropic's biggest intellectual property risk is that courts have not decided whether training AI on copyrighted material is fair use, so a loss even in a rival's case could force licenses or costly retraining. It already faces many suits over training data and outputs, including a $1.5B Bartz copyright settlement approved in July 2026 and pending music publisher and Reddit cases. Security incidents, including foreign government hacking, have already occurred; stolen model weights, the trained numbers that make up a model, would let rivals skip years of research and bypass safety controls. Privacy laws such as the GDPR, open source licenses, licensed technology, patent claims and hires from rivals carrying secrets add legal exposure.

paras.p576: Courts have not yet settled whether training AI on copyrighted material is legal "fair use," so a loss in any lawsuit, including one against another AI company, could force Anthropic to pay for licenses, stop distributing models, or retrain them at great cost.

s85.tldr: Courts have not yet decided whether training AI on copyrighted material counts as legal "fair use," so a loss in any lawsuit, even one brought against another AI company, could force Anthropic to pay for licenses, stop distributing its models, or retrain them at great cost.

paras.p577: Anthropic must follow many privacy laws, such as the EU's GDPR, that differ, conflict and are being newly applied to AI, while lawyers and state officials are already suing AI companies, which could force product changes, costs and fines.
paras.p578: Anthropic's privacy costs and exposure depend on how customers reach Claude and what data is involved, and the company has already faced operational errors or claims that its use of personal or confidential data, including in training, broke its obligations.
paras.p579: If data is exposed, altered or made unavailable, Anthropic may have to notify people, regulators or customers, adding legal and reputational risk.
paras.p580: Any real or apparent failure by Anthropic or its contractors to keep privacy promises or follow privacy law could bring investigations, lawsuits, fines, forced changes and lost customers.

s86.tldr: Anthropic must follow many privacy laws, such as the EU's GDPR, that differ, conflict and are newly being applied to AI, and lawyers and state officials are already suing AI companies. Its exposure depends on how customers reach Claude and what data is involved. It has already faced operational errors or claims that its use of personal or confidential data, including in training, broke its obligations. If data is exposed, altered or made unavailable, Anthropic may have to notify people, regulators or customers. Real or apparent failures by Anthropic or its contractors could bring investigations, lawsuits, fines, forced product changes and lost customers.

paras.p581: Anthropic's safety work sometimes requires collecting and processing personal and sensitive data, which raises the stakes of any leak and exposes it to laws being stretched to cover AI safety in unclear ways.

s87.tldr: Anthropic's safety work sometimes requires collecting and processing personal and sensitive data, which raises the stakes of any leak and exposes it to laws being stretched to cover AI safety in unclear ways.

paras.p582: Anthropic and its customers handle sensitive information, and cyberattacks and accidental exposures have already led to breaches, unauthorized access and other harms, and may do so again.
paras.p583: Foreign government hackers already target Anthropic, and its model weights, the trained numbers that make up a model, are prized espionage targets; Mythos, given its strong ability to find software vulnerabilities, may draw specific attacks.
paras.p584: Anthropic admits it has operated with known security gaps and may not stop the best funded government hackers; stolen model weights would let rivals skip years of research and use the models without Anthropic's safety controls.
paras.p585: Anthropic has already been targeted by job applicants using false identities, insiders could be bribed or coerced, and in some countries vendors or data center operators may be legally forced to secretly give governments access to its systems or weights.
paras.p586: Anthropic has already seen attacks on the software supply chain, meaning tools and code it gets from others, and geopolitical conflict may increase them, so it may not catch every attempt to steal data.
paras.p587: New AI features face AI specific attacks, such as hidden instructions in inputs, copying models through repeated queries, and poisoned training data, which standard defenses may miss, and Anthropic's countermeasures could wrongly block legitimate users.
paras.p588: Claude's agent products, which act on their own by running code, editing files, sending messages and making transactions, can be hijacked through manipulated web pages or data, possibly harming many customers at once with damage firewalls may not stop.
paras.p589: Anthropic has already found flaws, including hallucinations, meaning confident but false outputs, only after release, causing outages and harmful outputs, and even incidents caused by customers' own security mistakes can hurt Anthropic's reputation and expose it to liability.
paras.p590: Attackers have already used AI, including Anthropic's own models, to automate attacks and impersonate employees or executives, and may keep doing so against Anthropic, its customers and its partners.
paras.p591: Internal failures or breaches could cost Anthropic customers, and its offices and data centers, many run by others, face physical break ins that could bypass network defenses and reach its model weights.
paras.p592: Despite heavy spending on security, Anthropic cannot guarantee its defenses or responses will work, small incidents may later prove serious when added together, and fixing breaches could pull money away from growth.
paras.p593: A breach at Anthropic or a partner, especially a CSP, meaning a cloud provider such as Amazon, Google or Microsoft, could bring large costs, lawsuits and fines, and the liability limits in its terms may not hold up.
paras.p594: In the EU, Anthropic must report certain incidents to regulators under the GDPR, the NIS2 cybersecurity directive and the EU AI Act, which covers general purpose models with systemic risk, with more reporting duties coming for high risk systems.
paras.p595: US laws such as New York's SHIELD Act, New York's RAISE Act and the California Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act also require incident reporting, so late or inaccurate disclosures raise Anthropic's legal exposure.
paras.p596: Anthropic has some cyber insurance, but coverage may become unaffordable or unavailable, may not cover its losses, and insurers may pay late or refuse claims, leaving large losses uninsured.

s88.tldr: Security incidents have already happened at Anthropic: breaches, attacks by foreign government hackers, impostor job applicants, software supply chain attacks, and attacks automated with AI, including its own models. Its model weights, the trained numbers that make up a model, are prime espionage targets. Anthropic admits known security gaps and may not stop the best funded government hackers, and stolen weights would let rivals skip years of research and bypass its safety controls. Mythos may draw attacks because it is strong at finding software flaws. Claude's agents, which act on their own, can be hijacked and harm many customers at once. EU and US laws require incident reporting, and cyber insurance may not cover losses.

paras.p597: Anthropic trains Claude on internet data collected by automated crawlers, scanned books, licensed data and data its own models generate; it tries to respect website rules and paywalls but may fail, and poor records of data origins create legal risk.
paras.p598: Reddit has already sued Anthropic, claiming it improperly took posts from Reddit's platform; Anthropic moved the case to federal court on July 3, 2025, it was sent back to state court on March 30, 2026, and it remains pending.
paras.p599: Defending scraping lawsuits is expensive and distracting whether or not they have merit, and Anthropic may be unable to run its business in a way that avoids all such claims.
paras.p600: Settling such cases could force Anthropic to stop certain data collection methods and build costly replacements that may not work.
paras.p601: If a case goes to trial and Anthropic loses, a judgment that may not be overturned could require large payments or stopping some or all operations.

s89.tldr: Anthropic trains Claude on web data gathered by automated crawlers, scanned books, licensed data and data its own models generate. It tries to respect website rules and paywalls but may fail, and poor records of where data came from add legal risk. Reddit has already sued, claiming Anthropic improperly took its posts. Anthropic moved the case to federal court on July 3, 2025, it was sent back to state court on March 30, 2026, and it remains pending. Such suits are costly even without merit. Settlements could force Anthropic to drop collection methods and build costly substitutes, and losing at trial could mean large payments or halting some or all operations.

paras.p602: If Anthropic or the customers and partners supplying its data lack the rights to use that data, including for training, Anthropic could face claims forcing it to cut features, separate data or retrain models.
paras.p603: This repeats that defending data lawsuits is costly and distracting, and adds that because such claims can be very broad, Anthropic expects to face some as a normal part of business.

s90.tldr: If Anthropic, or the customers and partners who supply its data, lack the rights to use that data, including for training, Anthropic could face claims forcing it to cut features, separate data or retrain models. Such claims can be very broad and are costly to defend, and Anthropic expects to face some as a normal part of business.

paras.p604: Many companies and individuals, including firms that hold patents only to sue over them, may claim rights over technology Anthropic uses, and such claims become more likely as Anthropic grows more visible and competition increases.
paras.p605: Anthropic trains Claude on material that can include copyrighted work and already faces many lawsuits over training data and outputs, including a $1.5B copyright settlement in Bartz approved in July 2026, plus pending music publisher and Reddit suits with uncertain outcomes.
paras.p606: Anthropic also faces patent lawsuits that could bring large damages or court orders barring certain technologies, and rivals with much bigger patent collections could use them against Anthropic while limiting its ability to trade licenses or fight back.
paras.p607: Defending these suits is expensive and distracting even when the claims are weak, and Anthropic expects such intellectual property claims to be a routine part of doing business.
paras.p608: A settlement could force Anthropic to pay for licenses that may be costly or unavailable, leaving it to redesign its technology or stop the disputed practice, which could be expensive or fail.
paras.p609: If a case goes to trial and Anthropic loses, the judgment might not be overturned on appeal and could require large payments or halting some or all of its operations.
paras.p610: Anthropic promises to cover some customers, partners and outside model testers against infringement claims, sometimes with no limit on its liability, so it could end up paying damages, funding lawsuits or changing products on their behalf.

s91.tldr: Anthropic already faces many lawsuits over training data, which can include copyrighted work, and over Claude's outputs. These include a $1.5B copyright settlement in Bartz approved in July 2026 and pending music publisher and Reddit suits. Patent suits, including from firms that hold patents only to sue, could bring large damages or bans on technologies, and rivals with bigger patent holdings could use them against Anthropic. Such claims grow with its visibility, are costly even when weak, and are expected routinely. Settlements may require costly or unavailable licenses or redesigns, and trial losses could force large payments or halt operations. Anthropic also covers some customers, partners and model testers against such claims, sometimes without a liability limit.

paras.p611: Anthropic protects its technology through patents, copyrights, trademarks, trade secrets and contracts, but insiders with access to model weights (the learned settings that make Claude work), training data or research could steal them despite its controls.
paras.p612: Others have already infringed Anthropic's rights, and suing to stop them is costly, can provoke countersuits challenging its rights, and can expose confidential information through court evidence sharing, while weak protection lets competitors copy its models more easily.
paras.p613: Anthropic holds some patents and has applications pending, but new patents may not be granted, may be too narrow to give a real advantage, or may be challenged and overturned.
paras.p614: Because patent applications stay secret for a while after filing, Anthropic cannot be sure it invented or filed first, and it might unknowingly use technology that later infringes someone else's newly issued patent.
paras.p615: Much of Anthropic's technology is protected only as trade secrets backed by confidentiality agreements, which others could independently recreate or which employees and contractors could breach.
paras.p616: Third parties have already registered similar trademarks and opposed Anthropic's applications, and if its brand names are successfully challenged Anthropic could have to rebrand, losing recognition and spending on new marketing.

s92.tldr: Anthropic protects its technology with patents, copyrights, trademarks, trade secrets and contracts, but insiders could steal model weights (the learned settings that make Claude work), training data or research. Others have already infringed its rights. Suing them is costly, can provoke countersuits and can expose confidential information, while weak protection makes its models easier to copy. Its patents may not be granted, may be too narrow, or may be overturned, and because applications stay secret for a time, it may unknowingly infringe newly issued patents. Trade secrets can be recreated independently or leaked. Third parties have already registered similar trademarks and opposed its applications, which could force a costly rebrand.

paras.p617: Anthropic uses open-source software (free code shared under license terms), and breaking those terms, possibly without knowing it when its own Claude Code writes code, could force it to pay damages, rework software or publicly release proprietary code.
paras.p618: Open-source code comes without warranties and is written by outsiders, so it may contain hidden security flaws or errors that take time to fix and could hurt Claude's performance, reputation or feature launches.

s93.tldr: Anthropic uses open-source software, free code shared under license terms. Breaking those terms, possibly without knowing it when its own Claude Code writes code, could force it to pay damages, rework software or publicly release its proprietary code. This code comes without warranties from outside authors and may contain hidden security flaws or errors that hurt Claude's performance, reputation or feature launches.

paras.p619: Anthropic builds some licensed outside technology into its products, and if those licenses end, become too costly, or turn out to infringe others' rights, it may lack timely replacements and could have to limit what it sells.
paras.p620: Losing licensed technology could force Anthropic to build or buy weaker alternatives at higher cost, and poorly maintained outside software could introduce errors or security gaps into its products.

s94.tldr: Anthropic builds some licensed outside technology into its products. If those licenses end, become too costly or turn out to infringe others' rights, it may lack timely replacements, have to limit what it sells, or build or buy weaker, costlier alternatives. Poorly maintained outside software could also introduce errors or security gaps into its products.

paras.p621: As Anthropic builds its own tools to replace outside vendors, those vendors may sue, alleging breach of contract, intellectual property theft, misuse of confidential information or unfair competition.
paras.p622: Such vendor claims could be brought even without merit and lead to costly litigation, settlements or court orders limiting how Anthropic deploys or expands its products.

s95.tldr: As Anthropic builds its own tools to replace outside vendors, those vendors may sue, even without merit, alleging breach of contract, intellectual property theft, misuse of confidential information or unfair competition. That could lead to costly litigation, settlements or court orders limiting how Anthropic deploys or expands its products.

paras.p623: Anthropic competes hard for AI talent, has hired people from rival companies, and has lost staff to those rivals.
paras.p624: Employees hired from competitors may carry their former employers' secrets, so Anthropic could be accused of stealing trade secrets even without any intentional wrongdoing.
paras.p625: Such disputes could be costly and disruptive and could lead to damages, limits on certain technologies or employees' roles, and reputational harm.

s96.tldr: Anthropic competes hard for AI talent, hiring people from rival companies and losing staff to them. Employees hired from competitors may carry their former employers' secrets, so Anthropic could be accused of stealing trade secrets even without intentional wrongdoing. Such disputes could be costly and disruptive and could bring damages, limits on certain technologies or employees' roles, and reputational harm.

s97.tldr: Anthropic faces many lawsuits and government actions. Its safety cooperation with rivals carries antitrust risk, and a September 2026 proposed class action already accuses it and others of agreeing to slow model improvement. In June 2026 Commerce Department export restrictions forced it to shut off Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for all customers; its export controls have already failed and it has reported violations itself. Healthcare use, anti-bribery laws, an April 2025 Justice Department rule limiting data sharing with parties tied to China, and foreign laws such as the EU AI Act add risk. ESG scrutiny of AI's power and water use, plus payment fraud and chargebacks that have already cost it money, round out the exposures.

paras.p626: Anthropic faces a wide range of lawsuits and government actions, and new risks are emerging as Claude takes autonomous actions in the real world and as it moves into healthcare, where errors could harm patients and trigger regulation.
paras.p627: Anthropic's public calls to manage the pace of AI development and its safety collaborations with rivals carry antitrust risk, and in September 2026 a proposed class action already accused it and other AI developers of agreeing to slow model improvement.
paras.p628: Antitrust cases can bring triple damages and government investigations, and Anthropic's proposal for a narrow antitrust exemption for safety cooperation has drawn political opposition, which may push it to scale back safety collaboration it considers central to its mission.
paras.p629: The outcome of any legal or regulatory action is unpredictable, and even weak claims can scare off customers, delay contracts, damage partnerships and reputation, and consume management time.
paras.p630: Setting aside money for lawsuits involves guesswork, and as Bartz showed, Anthropic may settle even with good defenses and insurance may not cover the full cost, while it also must pay legal costs for some partners and executives.

s98.tldr: Anthropic faces many lawsuits and government actions. New risks are emerging as Claude takes autonomous actions and moves into healthcare, where errors could harm patients and bring regulation. Its public calls to manage the pace of AI development and its safety work with rivals carry antitrust risk. In September 2026 a proposed class action already accused Anthropic and other developers of agreeing to slow model improvement. Antitrust cases can bring triple damages and investigations, and political opposition to its proposed narrow antitrust exemption for safety cooperation may push it to scale that work back. Outcomes are unpredictable, and even weak claims can scare off customers. As Bartz showed, it may settle despite good defenses, and insurance may fall short.

paras.p631: Anthropic must follow strict, aggressively enforced anti-bribery and anti-money laundering laws in the United States, the United Kingdom and elsewhere that bar improper payments to officials and private parties.
paras.p632: Anthropic uses agents and intermediaries for sales and lobbying, including dealings with government and state-owned entities, and could be held responsible for their corrupt acts even if it never approved them.
paras.p633: Anthropic cannot guarantee its compliance policies will work or that no employee or partner has broken or will break these laws.
paras.p634: As international sales grow, so does the risk of violations, which could bring criminal penalties, large fines, loss of export rights or bans from U.S. government contracts, along with reputational damage and heavy defense costs.

s99.tldr: Anthropic must follow strict, aggressively enforced anti-bribery and anti-money laundering laws in the United States, the United Kingdom and elsewhere that bar improper payments to officials and private parties. It uses agents and intermediaries for sales and lobbying, including with government and state-owned entities, and could be held liable for their corrupt acts even if it never approved them. Its compliance policies may not prevent violations. Growing international sales raise the risk of criminal penalties, large fines, loss of export rights, bans from U.S. government contracts, reputational damage and heavy defense costs.

paras.p635: Anthropic's models, platform and apps fall under U.S. export rules run by the Commerce Department, and sometimes the State Department's weapons rules (ITAR); because the models and the rules both keep changing, which rules apply is uncertain, and some access may need government permission, even for certain foreign nationals inside the U.S.
paras.p636: Because Anthropic's products use encryption to protect data, and future models might be able to write software that is itself export controlled, more of its products could need government permission before being sent or offered abroad.
paras.p637: Most of Anthropic's products can be exported without a license, but in June 2026 the Commerce Department restricted the Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models worldwide, so Anthropic shut them off for all customers until safeguards were updated and the restrictions lifted, and similar actions could recur, last longer, and cost customers and market share.
paras.p638: U.S. and foreign sanctions bar dealings with certain people and countries and can change with little notice, and U.S. rules on technology tied to designated adversary countries could limit which suppliers Anthropic can use for its data centers and chips, raising costs or delaying projects.
paras.p639: Anthropic blocks access from certain countries by internet address, screens some customers and vendors against restricted lists, and writes compliance terms into contracts, but these controls have failed before, it has already reported violations to authorities itself, and outsiders have already gotten around its controls.
paras.p640: If Anthropic breaks export or sanctions rules, it could face criminal or civil penalties, large fines, loss of export rights, exclusion from U.S. government contracts and bad press, and fighting any investigation would be costly and distracting for management.
paras.p641: If foreign customers use Anthropic less or Anthropic is limited in selling abroad, revenue from countries where it cannot operate could fall and hurt the business.
paras.p642: Anthropic could also suffer reputational damage, investigations or penalties if its partners, vendors, customers or contractors break export or sanctions rules, or if it fails to get them to commit contractually to follow those rules.
paras.p643: Violations, or even apparent violations, could cost Anthropic the right to sell to the U.S. government and other public bodies, and the work of checking compliance itself can slow down or lose individual deals.
paras.p644: Other countries also restrict encryption and technology trade, as shown by the sanctions placed on Russia, Belarus and parts of Ukraine after Russia's invasion, and new or wider rules could reduce foreign use of Anthropic's products, slow expansion and lower revenue.

s100.tldr: In June 2026 the U.S. Commerce Department restricted Anthropic's Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models worldwide, so Anthropic shut them off for all customers until the restrictions lifted; such actions could recur and cost customers. U.S. export rules, sometimes including weapons rules, cover its products, and encryption and future software-writing abilities could require more government licenses, even for some foreign nationals in the U.S. Rules on adversary-linked technology could limit chip and data center suppliers. Anthropic's controls have already failed, it has reported violations itself, and outsiders have evaded them. Violations by Anthropic or its partners could bring fines, criminal penalties and lost government contracts. Compliance checks slow deals, and foreign trade limits like those on Russia could cut revenue.

paras.p645: Anthropic already operates in the UK, the EU, Canada and Asia-Pacific and expects growth to depend partly on new countries, which brings different legal, economic and political risks; a list of specific ones follows.
paras.p646: Selling abroad means adapting Claude and Anthropic's products to each country, including translating them into other languages, which costs money.
paras.p647: Countries have their own privacy, export and sanctions rules that can conflict with each other, and some require customer data to be kept inside their borders.
paras.p648: Some countries' laws can force Anthropic's staff, suppliers or data center operators to hand systems or data to the government, sometimes without telling Anthropic and with little way to push back.
paras.p649: A Department of Justice rule in effect since April 2025 limits or bans sharing certain data with partners, vendors, employees or investors tied to China and other named countries, which may force Anthropic to renegotiate contracts.
paras.p650: Trade barriers such as tariffs, customs duties and retaliatory measures by the U.S. and other governments can raise Anthropic's costs.
paras.p651: Fast-changing laws on AI, data, cybersecurity and online services, such as the EU AI Act and the UK Online Safety Act 2023, require constant compliance work and can carry large fines.
paras.p652: Hiring abroad often relies on outside firms that legally employ staff on Anthropic's behalf, and if these setups or late local entities break labor or tax rules, Anthropic faces fines and back-pay claims.
paras.p653: Keeping a consistent company culture is harder when staff are spread across many countries.
paras.p654: Setting up foreign subsidiaries, bank accounts, payroll and benefits takes government approvals and time, and delays can slow local hiring.
paras.p655: Some deals with foreign companies may need approval from the U.S. or other governments.
paras.p656: Foreign markets may bring lower prices, slower sales, slower customer payments and trouble collecting what is owed.
paras.p657: New countries bring new competitors Anthropic does not face at home.
paras.p658: Anthropic's technology and other legal rights are harder to protect and enforce in many countries outside the United States.
paras.p659: Some countries' laws and business habits favor local companies over Anthropic.
paras.p660: Following many overlapping and changing national laws on copyright, employment, tax, privacy, export controls and sanctions is complex and hard to get right.
paras.p661: People abroad may try to get around sanctions and export controls to use Anthropic's technology, creating legal exposure for the company.
paras.p662: Operating in more countries makes Anthropic's accounting and financial reporting more burdensome and complicated.
paras.p663: Building offices and data center infrastructure in many countries is expensive.
paras.p664: If foreign currencies fall against the U.S. dollar, money Anthropic earns abroad is worth less in dollars.
paras.p665: Some countries restrict moving money out, which could trap Anthropic's funds.
paras.p666: Foreign operations could lead to unfavorable tax outcomes.
paras.p667: Lawsuits and claims abroad bring costs and uncertain results.
paras.p668: New accounting rules or policy changes could alter how Anthropic reports its results.
paras.p669: Tax laws in various countries could change in ways that hurt Anthropic.
paras.p670: Local economic slowdowns and political events in the countries where Anthropic operates could affect its business.
paras.p671: Many governments now review foreign investments and takeovers, which could limit who can invest in Anthropic and its ability to fund overseas data center partners or buy foreign companies, technology and talent.
paras.p672: Rising geopolitical tension, especially U.S. scrutiny of Chinese state actors' access to AI, could restrict where and to whom Anthropic sells, shrink its market, raise costs, and bring penalties if foreign states misuse its models.
paras.p673: Anthropic's overseas growth depends on managing all these risks, which will take substantial management time and money, and failure could limit its growth.

s101.tldr: Anthropic already operates in the UK, the EU, Canada and Asia-Pacific and expects growth to depend partly on new countries, which will demand substantial management time and money. Risks include conflicting privacy, export and sanctions rules, requirements to keep data in the country, and laws forcing staff or data center operators to hand data to governments. A Department of Justice rule in effect since April 2025 limits data sharing with parties tied to China and other named countries. Further risks include tariffs, laws such as the EU AI Act and the UK Online Safety Act 2023, labor and tax issues, weaker protection of its technology, currency losses, trapped funds and foreign investment reviews. U.S. scrutiny of Chinese state access to AI could shrink its market.

paras.p674: Governments, investors and the public are scrutinizing ESG (environmental, social and governance) practices, especially AI's heavy use of power, water and critical minerals, and some investors may avoid Anthropic if they judge its record weak.
paras.p675: Climate disclosure rules in California, the EU and the UK will take significant effort to meet, while anti-ESG policies in the U.S. could expose those same practices to lawsuits and government challenges.
paras.p676: Anthropic could lose investors to competitors seen as more responsible and could face backlash, activism or litigation from groups who dislike its positions, or its silence, on sensitive issues.

s102.tldr: Governments, investors and the public are scrutinizing ESG (environmental, social and governance) practices, especially AI's heavy use of power, water and critical minerals. Some investors may avoid Anthropic or prefer competitors seen as more responsible. Climate disclosure rules in California, the EU and the UK will take significant effort to meet, while U.S. anti-ESG policies could expose those same practices to lawsuits and government challenges. paras.p717: Anthropic's new charter and bylaws contain several features that make it harder for anyone to take over the company; the list follows.
paras.p718: Through separate share classes, the Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT) and the Founder LLC can elect the whole board, and the Founder LLC alone can decide every shareholder vote, including any merger or sale, for the foreseeable future.
paras.p719: Until the Class F Sunset Time, when the founders' special voting class ends, open board seats not reserved for Trust directors are filled on the Founder LLC's instruction or by a vote of Class A and Class F holders.
paras.p720: Until the Class T Sunset Time, when the Trust's special class ends, changing the size of the board needs approval from 80% of authorized directors, which makes it hard to add seats to shift control.
paras.p721: Only specific people can call a special shareholder meeting, such as the board majority, the chair, the CEO, the President, or the Founder LLC before its sunset, so ordinary shareholders cannot force one.
paras.p722: Shareholders can act by written consent instead of a meeting only for limited matters such as director elections while the special classes exist, and not at all after both sunset times, which limits quick shareholder action.
paras.p723: Class A shareholders must follow advance notice rules to nominate directors or raise proposals at the annual meeting.
paras.p724: After the founders' special class ends, the board will be split into three groups serving staggered three-year terms, so control cannot be replaced in a single election.
paras.p725: After the founders' special class ends, changing certain charter and bylaw provisions will need two-thirds (66 2/3%) of Class A voting power, a higher bar than a simple majority.
paras.p726: Shareholders cannot concentrate all their votes on one director candidate, which makes it harder for minority holders to win a board seat.
paras.p727: The board can create new preferred stock with terms it sets, with approval from 80% of directors and, before the sunset, the Founder LLC's consent, a tool that could be used to resist a takeover.
paras.p728: Together these features could block or delay a change of control, make proxy fights and shareholder-driven changes harder, and so reduce the chance of shareholders receiving a takeover premium and possibly lower what investors will pay.

s121.tldr: Anthropic's new charter and bylaws make a takeover hard. Through special share classes, the Long-Term Benefit Trust and the Founder LLC can elect the whole board, and the Founder LLC alone can decide every shareholder vote, including any merger or sale, for the foreseeable future. Other barriers include an 80% director vote to change board size, no shareholder right to call special meetings, limited written consent and advance notice rules. Once the founders' class ends, the board becomes staggered and some changes need two thirds of Class A votes. There is no vote pooling on one candidate, and the board can create preferred stock. These features could cut takeover premiums and the share price.
