paras.p861: This opens management's own explanation of the financial results, warning that it contains forward-looking predictions that may prove wrong and that past results from 2023 through 2025 do not guarantee future performance.

s137.tldr: Revenue rose from $41 million in 2023 to $16.286B in the first half of 2026. Over the same span, compute, the data center chips that train and run Claude, fell from 1,056% to 55% of revenue. The June 2026 quarter brought Anthropic's first operating income, $974 million. Net losses came mostly from revaluing convertible notes. Customers paying $100,000 or more grew to over 11,900. Anthropic expects margins to shrink as new compute arrives and growth to slow. Commitments, mostly take or pay, include about $114.5B with Google, $110.0B with Amazon and $161.2B of Broadcom hardware rent. About $26.6B of unrecorded stock pay will start hitting results at the IPO. An estimated 5% to 7% of recent revenue came from rule breaking customers.

paras.p862: Anthropic describes itself as a research lab founded in 2021 with a mission of developing advanced AI safely for humanity's long-term benefit, and says Claude's revenue grew from $0 at launch in early 2023 to an undisclosed figure for the quarter ended September 30, 2026.

s138.tldr: Anthropic describes itself as a research lab founded in 2021 with a mission of developing advanced AI safely for humanity's long-term benefit, and says Claude's revenue grew from $0 at launch in early 2023 to an undisclosed figure for the quarter ended September 30, 2026.

paras.p863: Anthropic says four main factors drive its financial results, listed below.
paras.p864: The first factor is customer uptake: each more capable Claude model attracts new customers and leads existing ones to use it for more tasks, which raises revenue.
paras.p865: The second factor is getting more model capability and revenue from each dollar spent on compute, the specialized chips in data centers that train and run Claude, where Anthropic says it has already improved substantially.
paras.p866: The third factor is running the company lean, with skilled staff, efficient selling and heavy internal use of Claude, which Anthropic says lifts profit margins and revenue per employee.
paras.p867: The fourth factor is continued heavy spending on compute, which Anthropic considers essential for long-term growth and plans to keep doing.
paras.p868: Revenue and efficiency rise steadily, but compute costs arrive in large chunks when new capacity comes online, so spending is booked well before the revenue that capacity eventually brings in.
paras.p869: Operating margins expanded sharply in the nine months ended September 30, 2026, but Anthropic expects them to shrink, sometimes significantly, whenever large new compute arrives, so profits will swing from period to period.
paras.p870: Most compute is reserved 12 to 18 months ahead under multi-year contracts, and when demand outruns it Anthropic buys pricier short-term capacity; it expects to do more of this soon, which will squeeze margins.

s139.tldr: Anthropic says four factors drive its results: more capable Claude models winning customers and wider use, more capability and revenue per dollar of compute (the data center chips that train and run Claude), lean operations with heavy internal use of Claude, and continued heavy compute spending. Compute costs arrive in large chunks when capacity comes online, before the revenue it brings. Operating margins expanded sharply in the nine months ended September 30, 2026, but Anthropic expects them to shrink, sometimes significantly, when new compute arrives. Most compute is reserved 12 to 18 months ahead under multi-year contracts; when demand outruns it, Anthropic buys pricier short term capacity, which it expects to do more of soon.

paras.p871: Anthropic says each Claude model is built to lead on coding, autonomous task handling, computer use and reasoning, which drives demand, and it sells through its own teams, Amazon, Google and Microsoft clouds, and consulting and data partners.
paras.p872: Anthropic sells models at different price and speed levels, a developer platform and ready-made apps, and over 50% of its customers paying $100,000 or more yearly used both platform and apps in the September 2026 quarter, up from about 30% in December 2025.
paras.p873: Customers paying $100,000 or more over the past twelve months rose from more than 950 at September 30, 2025 to more than 11,900 a year later, with more than 1,900 above $1 million and about 250 above $10 million.
paras.p874: Net Revenue Retention of about 900% at September 30, 2026 means existing customers, taken as a group, are spending roughly nine times what they spent a year earlier.
paras.p875: Anthropic says businesses are building Claude into core operations, yet AI adoption across the economy is still early, and it expects its market to grow as Claude improves.

s140.tldr: Customers paying Anthropic $100,000 or more over twelve months rose from more than 950 at September 30, 2025 to more than 11,900 a year later, with more than 1,900 above $1 million and about 250 above $10 million, and existing customers as a group spent about nine times what they did a year earlier. Anthropic builds each Claude model to lead in coding, autonomous tasks, computer use and reasoning, and sells it at several price levels as a developer platform and ready-made apps through its own teams, cloud providers and partners. Over 50% of large customers used both in the September 2026 quarter, up from about 30% in December 2025. It says economy wide adoption remains early.

paras.p876: Paying for compute, meaning the specialized chips in data centers that train and run Claude, is Anthropic's largest operating cost, and the company says it now gets more model capability and more revenue out of each dollar spent on it than before.
paras.p877: Anthropic defines compute efficiency as getting the most intelligence and revenue per dollar of chips and data centers, and names three areas that drive it, listed next.
paras.p878: Anthropic's researchers keep finding ways to train models with less compute, and Claude itself now helps build the next Claude, which the company calls "closing the loop" and expects to compound across model generations.
paras.p879: Anthropic has cut the compute needed to run its models for customers at a given quality, which matters because demand has consistently exceeded the compute it has, so each saving lets it serve more customers and earn more.
paras.p880: Anthropic runs Claude on four chip families from Amazon, Google, NVIDIA and AMD using its own software to shift work to the cheapest suitable hardware, which reduces reliance on any one supplier and, it believes, is hard for rivals to copy.
paras.p881: Anthropic's revenue grew 1,368% year over year in the three months ended June 30, 2026, while compute and infrastructure costs grew 300%, and it has already released models including Mythos 5, Fable 5 and Opus 5 and products including Claude Cowork and Claude Design.

s141.tldr: Compute, the specialized data center chips that run Claude, is Anthropic's largest operating cost, and it now gets more capability and revenue per dollar: in the three months ended June 30, 2026, revenue grew 1,368% year over year while compute and infrastructure costs grew 300%. Researchers keep cutting training compute, and Claude now helps build the next Claude, gains Anthropic expects to compound. Serving customers needs less compute, letting Anthropic meet more demand, which has outrun supply. Its software routes work across Amazon, Google, NVIDIA and AMD chips to the cheapest fit, limiting supplier reliance. It has already released Mythos 5, Fable 5, Opus 5, Claude Cowork and Claude Design, among others.

paras.p882: Anthropic says Claude itself boosts staff productivity: over 90% of code changes in September 2026 were written by Claude, and code per engineer per day in the September 2026 quarter was over 45 times the 2024 average.
paras.p883: Over the year to September 30, 2026, twelve-month revenue grew about 1,200% while staff grew about 170%, lifting revenue per employee from $1.4 million to over $6.6 million.
paras.p884: Because customers find Claude themselves and partners resell it, Anthropic says its revenue can grow faster than its sales staff, making its selling cheaper than at typical business software firms.
paras.p885: Revenue rose from $1.2B to $16.3B for the six months ended June 30, 2025 and 2026, the operating loss shrank from $2.1B to $693 million, and Anthropic's adjusted measure swung from a $1.8B loss to $1.6B profit.

s142.tldr: Anthropic says Claude boosts its own productivity: Claude wrote over 90% of its code changes in September 2026, and code per engineer per day was over 45 times the 2024 average. Over the year to September 30, 2026, twelve month revenue grew about 1,200% while staff grew about 170%, lifting revenue per employee from $1.4 million to over $6.6 million. Because customers find Claude themselves and partners resell it, its selling costs less than at typical business software firms. In the first half of 2026 versus 2025, revenue rose from $1.2B to $16.3B, the operating loss shrank from $2.1B to $693 million, and the adjusted measure swung from a $1.8B loss to $1.6B profit.

paras.p886: Anthropic says it must keep spending heavily on compute, the specialized chips in data centers that train and run Claude, and more of that spending now goes to building its own infrastructure, paid well before it earns revenue, which will consume significant cash for the foreseeable future.
paras.p887: Anthropic has begun adding Anthropic Direct, leasing chips itself and placing them in dedicated facilities run for it, alongside cloud contracts, so it can reserve slow-to-build data centers early and delay the costlier chip purchases until its needs are clearer.
paras.p888: Anthropic has already signed purchase and lease commitments stretching to 2045, though this draft leaves the total and the near-term amounts blank; much of it is for Anthropic Direct, which lets cheaper long-term capacity replace short-term compute bought during demand spikes.
paras.p889: Anthropic plans to pay for these commitments with its revenue, cash, investments, a bank credit line, financing and equity promised by strategic partners, and the money from this IPO, but every dollar amount and the share price are still blank in this draft.

s143.tldr: Anthropic must keep spending heavily on compute, the specialized chips in data centers that train and run Claude, and a growing share now goes to building its own infrastructure, paid well before it earns revenue and expected to consume significant cash for the foreseeable future. Alongside cloud contracts, it has begun Anthropic Direct, leasing chips itself in dedicated facilities run for it, so it can reserve slow-to-build data centers early, delay costlier chip purchases until needs are clearer, and replace short-term compute bought during demand spikes with cheaper long-term capacity. It has already signed commitments stretching to 2045, mostly for Anthropic Direct, and plans to fund them with revenue, cash, investments, a bank credit line, partner financing and equity, and IPO proceeds. This draft leaves the totals, near-term amounts and share price blank.

paras.p890: Anthropic sells four model tiers, Mythos (including Fable), Opus, Sonnet and Haiku, trading capability against cost and speed; spending depends on which model and how much use, and customers can buy directly or through cloud provider marketplaces.
paras.p891: Most revenue comes from pay-per-use pricing, where customers are billed by tokens, the small chunks of text Claude processes, at rates set by the model chosen.
paras.p892: Anthropic also sells subscriptions to its apps for businesses and individual power users, with fixed usage allowances over terms usually 12 months or less.
paras.p893: Customers can combine subscription and pay-per-use, so subscribers who hit their usage limit either upgrade or pay extra, turning subscriptions into a source of added usage revenue.
paras.p894: More large customers are signing annual or multi-year contracts they cannot cancel, promising minimum spending in exchange for fixed prices, and these mostly produce pay-per-use revenue.
paras.p895: Pay-per-use revenue grew from $288 million (75%) in 2024 to $3.8B (83%) in 2025 and $13.1B (80%) in the first half of 2026, while subscriptions grew from $98 million to $789 million to $3.2B.
paras.p896: Anthropic warns its recent growth may reflect a young market and early customer enthusiasm that may not last, and expects its growth rate to slow, possibly sharply and sooner than expected.

s144.tldr: Most of Anthropic's revenue comes from pay per use billing by tokens, the small chunks of text Claude processes: $288 million (75%) in 2024, $3.8B (83%) in 2025 and $13.1B (80%) in the first half of 2026. Subscriptions grew from $98 million to $789 million to $3.2B, with fixed allowances and terms usually 12 months or less, and users who hit limits upgrade or pay extra. Customers choose among Mythos (including Fable), Opus, Sonnet and Haiku, trading capability against cost and speed, and buy directly or through cloud marketplaces. More large customers sign noncancellable minimum spending contracts. Anthropic warns growth may reflect early enthusiasm and expects it to slow, possibly sharply.

s145.tldr: Anthropic says Claude spreads cheaply because individuals, especially software developers using Claude Code, bring it into their employers, with sales teams arriving later to win company wide rollouts; sales, marketing and partnership spending was 19% of revenue for the six months ended June 30, 2026. Customers range from the largest companies to startups and nonprofits and often expand from coding into legal, finance and customer service. Applied AI engineers build custom solutions. Amazon, Google and Microsoft resell Claude while Anthropic keeps the contract, sets prices and pays each a fee. Consultancies and data platforms build on Claude, and Ode with Anthropic, launched with private equity firms, serves mid-sized companies.

paras.p897: Claude's customers range from the largest companies to startups and nonprofits worldwide, gaining value through more productive staff, faster processes and AI inside their own products, and their feedback shapes Anthropic's product plans.
paras.p898: Software developers were Anthropic's first and most demanding users, and its coding tool Claude Code has spread through major companies, often starting with individual engineers who then pushed wider adoption.
paras.p899: Individual users who use Claude for their own work matter because they often bring it into their employers, feeding enterprise sales.
paras.p900: Anthropic says growth spans coding, finance, writing and other office work, and customers that start with one use often expand to legal, finance, customer service and more.

s146.tldr: Claude's customers range from the largest companies to startups and nonprofits worldwide. They gain value from more productive staff, faster processes and AI built into their own products, and their feedback shapes Anthropic's product plans. Software developers were the first and most demanding users. The coding tool Claude Code has spread through major companies, often starting with individual engineers who pushed wider adoption. Individual users matter because they often bring Claude into their employers, feeding enterprise sales. Anthropic says growth spans coding, finance, writing and other office work, and customers that start with one use often expand to legal, finance, customer service and more.

s147.tldr: Anthropic says it spreads Claude cheaply: sales, marketing and partnership spending was 19% of revenue for the six months ended June 30, 2026. It says Claude's capability drives adoption, as individuals spread it within organizations, a pattern central to its revenue growth. Sales teams often arrive after Claude is already in use and win executive backing for company-wide rollouts. Applied AI engineers build custom solutions for selected customers and gather product feedback. Amazon, Google and Microsoft clouds resell Claude through their large sales forces, while Anthropic keeps the contract, sets prices and pays each a fee, keeping the gains from cheaper compute. Consulting firms and data platform partners also build on Claude. Anthropic has launched Ode with Anthropic with private equity firms to serve mid-sized companies.

s148.tldr: Anthropic's performance hinges on staying at the AI frontier: models released in the six months ended September 30, 2026 produced over 80% of that quarter's revenue. That requires vast compute whose supply it cannot control, so it is adding Anthropic Direct, leasing chips itself, and it needs funding on good terms. Customers paying $100,000 or more grew from about 20 at December 31, 2023 to over 11,900, plus about 40 million smaller payers, and no customer exceeded 10% of revenue. Holiday dips, such as a 20% drop in the two weeks ended January 2, 2026, will show more as growth slows. Its 5% share gift to its Public Benefit Fund and $541 million of 2025 donation matching dilute holders and add costs.

paras.p909: Anthropic believes companies pick the most capable and trustworthy AI, so its revenue growth depends partly on keeping its models at the cutting edge.
paras.p910: Anthropic says most customers switch to each new top model and expand their spending with it, linking model quality directly to revenue.
paras.p911: Staying at the frontier will require continued spending on research and compute, top engineers and enough funding to keep growing.

s149.tldr: Anthropic believes companies pick the most capable and trustworthy AI, so its revenue growth depends partly on keeping its models at the cutting edge. It says most customers switch to each new top model and expand their spending with it, which ties model quality directly to revenue. Staying ahead will require continued spending on research and compute, the specialized chips in data centers that train and run Claude. It will also need top engineers and enough funding to keep growing.

paras.p912: Anthropic needs vast compute and buys from several chip makers to limit dependence, but supply, power, data centers and export rules are outside its control, demand has outrun supply, and some cloud suppliers are also investors and competitors.

paras.p914: Anthropic constantly moves compute among research, customers and internal use and seeks techniques that get more output per chip, which will shape both its innovation pace and financial results.

s150.tldr: Anthropic needs vast compute and buys from several chip makers to limit dependence. paras.p1141: Before the IPO, the board estimated the common stock's value using an accounting industry guide and the factors listed below.
paras.p1142: One factor is independent valuations done at the time.
paras.p1143: Another is prices investors paid for Anthropic's shares, including in secondary sales and tender offers.
paras.p1144: Another is the extra rights preferred shareholders have over common shareholders.
paras.p1145: Another is actual and forecast financial performance.
paras.p1146: Another is the company's stage of development.
paras.p1147: Another is the outlook for the industry.
paras.p1148: Another is that private common stock is hard to sell.
paras.p1149: Another is the chance of an IPO or sale of the company given market conditions.
paras.p1150: Another is the business's history, industry trends and competition.
paras.p1151: Another is the broader economy, including growth, inflation, unemployment and interest rates.
paras.p1152: The board valued the whole company mainly from the price of the nearest funding round, then divided that value among share classes.
paras.p1153: To divide value among share classes, Anthropic blended an option pricing approach that treats each class as a claim on assets with an approach assuming all preferred shares convert to common.
paras.p1154: A discount was then applied because private shares are hard to sell, and recent share sales were also considered.
paras.p1155: These valuations rest on subjective assumptions about revenue, costs, discount rates and future events, and changing them could materially change the estimated stock value.
paras.p1156: After the IPO, the market price will replace these internal estimates.

s252.tldr: Before the IPO, Anthropic's board valued the whole company mainly from the price of the nearest funding round. It divided that value among share classes by blending two methods: one treats each class as a claim on assets, the other assumes all preferred shares convert to common. It then applied a discount because private shares are hard to sell. The board also weighed independent valuations, prior share sales including tender offers, preferred shareholders' extra rights, results and forecasts, the industry outlook, the chances of an IPO or sale, and the broader economy. These subjective assumptions could materially change the estimates. After the IPO, the market price will replace them.

paras.p1157: Anthropic chose to carry its convertible notes, which are loans that can turn into shares, at their current estimated market value. Any change in that value hits its reported profit or loss, which avoids splitting each note into a debt piece and a stock piece.
paras.p1158: Under its 2023 and 2024 note agreements with Amazon and Google, Anthropic also records its promises to issue more convertible notes later as liabilities, valued at current estimated worth, with value changes flowing into reported profit or loss.
paras.p1159: To value the notes, Anthropic combines two valuation methods, called CCA and CSE, that weigh how likely each outcome is: conversion into preferred stock or Class N common stock, repayment in cash at maturity, or a premium cash payout if Anthropic is acquired.
paras.p1160: These valuations rest on uncertain guesses about the timing and odds of a funding round, IPO, or sale, Anthropic's share value, and how much debt converts versus rolls into new interest-free notes, so reported results can swing materially when assumptions change.
paras.p1161: Anthropic issued SAFEs, which are investments that later convert into shares, in 2023 and valued them the same way, but all converted into preferred stock during 2023 and 2024, so none were outstanding afterward and the remaining valuation uncertainty involves the convertible and rollover notes.
paras.p1162: This points readers to Note 9 of the financial statements for full details on each convertible note, derivative liability, and SAFE, including their terms, conversions, and balances.

s253.tldr: Anthropic carries its convertible notes, loans convertible into shares, at estimated market value rather than splitting them into debt and stock, so value changes flow into reported profit or loss and results can swing materially as assumptions shift. Promises to issue more notes under 2023 and 2024 agreements with Amazon and Google are treated the same way. Values depend on the odds of conversion into preferred or Class N common stock, repayment at maturity, or a premium payout in a sale, and on guesses about deal timing, share value and rollovers into new interest-free notes. 2023 SAFEs, investments that convert into shares, were valued similarly but all became preferred stock by 2024.

s258.tldr: Anthropic argues AI could change the economy more than electricity or the internet. It predicts that within a few years, "Powerful AI" will work at top expert level on its own for hours to weeks. June 2026 quarter revenue was $11.6B, up 1,368%, turning a loss into $1.0B of operating income. Over 11,900 customers paid $100,000 or more, including every Fortune 10 company. Anthropic sells models, a platform and apps such as Claude Code and Cowork, directly and through Amazon, Google and Microsoft. It pools chips from four makers under commitments to 2045. Safety rules have already limited releases such as Mythos. Legal issues include a government ban after it refused surveillance and autonomous weapons uses, and the $1.5B Bartz settlement.

s259.tldr: Anthropic argues AI could change the economy more than electricity or the internet, if its risks are well managed. Revenue reached $11.6B in the quarter ended June 30, 2026, up 1,368% from $787 million a year earlier. Compute costs, the chips and data centers that train and run Claude, rose 300%, so a $1.2B operating loss became $1.0B of operating income, an 8% margin. In the year to September 30, 2026, over 11,900 customers paid at least $100,000 and about 250 paid $10 million. Anthropic held $112.4B in cash and $19.3B in short term investments at June 30. It cites its safety mission, its talent, one chip pool from AWS, Google, NVIDIA and AMD with commitments to 2045, and its business focus. Claude now writes most of Anthropic's code, which the company calls potentially dangerous.

s260.tldr: Anthropic says one mission guides how it directs its people, research and spending on chips: AI must become safer and more capable together. It argues this mission and a modest, truth seeking culture help it attract and keep top researchers and engineers. It combines capability and safety research, uses each Claude model to help build the next, which it calls "closing the loop", and sometimes deliberately slows releases to manage risk. It manages compute from AWS, Google, NVIDIA and AMD as one shared pool, with commitments running to 2045 whose totals are blank in this draft. It focuses on business customers, where it believes AI creates the most economic value.

Claude is moving from single answers to long professional tasks through three main products: Claude Platform, tools to build on Claude; Claude Code, an agent that does full software work; and Claude Cowork, which operates a computer for office tasks. Beyond adoption without sales effort, Anthropic sells through the Amazon, Google and Microsoft clouds, consultancies, data platforms and Ode, a venture for midsized companies.

s262.tldr: Revenue reached $11.6B in the quarter ended June 30, 2026, up 1,368% from $787 million a year earlier. Over the same period, compute and infrastructure costs (the chips and data centers that train and run Claude) rose 300%. Anthropic swung from a $1.2B operating loss, a margin of minus 152%, to $1.0B of operating income, an 8% margin. On its own adjusted measure it went from a $1.0B loss to $2.2B of income, a 19% margin. As of September 30, 2026, existing customers' spending had grown about 900%, and revenue per employee topped $6.6 million, up from $1.4 million. As of June 30, 2026, Anthropic had raised $141.1B and held $112.4B in cash plus $19.3B in short term investments. It admits multiyear compute bets are risky.

s263.tldr: Anthropic claims its size and growth feed two cycles that keep improving Claude and protect its lead. In the first, customer use reveals hard problems, Anthropic improves its products to solve them, and better products spread further and generate new feedback. In the second, revenue from business customers pays for chips, research and staff. That investment improves Claude, customers then use it for more tasks, and the extra revenue is reinvested.

paras.p1202: Anthropic says Claude now does much of the work of building the next Claude, including running experiments, preparing training data, testing models and writing code, and that this cycle is speeding up its discovery of compute multipliers, meaning techniques that get more capability from the same chips.
paras.p1203: Inside Anthropic, Claude Code, its product that writes and runs software on its own, solved about 90% of hard, loosely defined engineering problems by September 2026, up about 50 points in nine months, and wrote over 90% of September 2026 code contributions.
paras.p1204: Between December 31, 2024 and September 30, 2026, Anthropic's staff grew more than five times while quarterly revenue grew 86 times, comparing the quarter ended September 30, 2026 with the quarter ended December 31, 2024.
paras.p1205: Anthropic attributes revenue growing much faster than headcount to employees across research, engineering, sales and operations using groups of Claude agents, letting a relatively small workforce do work that would normally need many more people.
paras.p1206: Anthropic's own use of Claude, valued at list prices, grew over 250 times from January to September 2026 and since April 2026 has exceeded its monthly payroll costs excluding stock pay, so a large share of compute now goes to internal use that Anthropic expects to keep speeding development.
paras.p1207: Anthropic acknowledges that using AI to build better AI could be seriously dangerous if progress speeds up sharply, and says its Responsible Scaling Policy, its internal safety framework, covers monitoring and limiting the risks of AI improving itself.

s264.tldr: Anthropic says Claude does much of building the next Claude, speeding discovery of ways to get more capability from the same chips. Claude Code, which writes and runs software on its own, solved about 90% of hard engineering problems by September 2026, up about 50 points in nine months, writing over 90% of September code. From December 2024 to September 2026, staff grew over fivefold and quarterly revenue 86-fold, credited to staff using Claude agents. Internal Claude use, at list prices, grew over 250-fold from January to September 2026, has topped payroll excluding stock pay since April, and absorbs much chip capacity. Sonnet balances performance, cost and speed for general tasks, including helper agents. Haiku is the cheapest and fastest class, built for high volume work.

s341.tldr: Anthropic's governance is built to protect its mission and leaves public shareholders little control. As a Delaware public benefit corporation, its board must balance profits, affected people and its purpose. It will publish a report on its goals at least every two years. The Long-Term Benefit Trust holds Class T stock that elects most of the board. Its trustees are paid $400,000 a year each, may not own stock and include Neil Shah, Ben Bernanke and two others, with one seat vacant. The seven co-founders' single Class F share holds 50.1% of votes and is never diluted. It ends if fewer than three founders remain for 90 days. Changing the trust needs high approvals, such as 80% of the board and trustees.

paras.p1517: Anthropic created the Long-Term Benefit Trust, an independent body of trustees with expertise in AI safety, security, and policy, set up so that trustees have little financial stake in the company and can judge the profit versus mission balance freely.

s343.tldr: The Long-Term Benefit Trust, a body of independent AI safety and policy experts, holds Class T stock that elects and removes most of Anthropic's board, which gives it effective influence over mergers or a sale. The stock carries no right to profits. Trustees may not hold Anthropic securities and are paid a fixed $400,000 a year each. Anthropic could rewrite or cancel the trust's powers without payment, but only with high approvals, such as 80% of both the board and the trustees. Without trustee support, it needs founder and shareholder votes, and later 85% of all Class A shares. The trustees are Chair Neil Shah, Richard Fontaine, Ben Bernanke and Christopher Stubbs, with one seat vacant. Anthropic funds the trust, paying $8,425,213 in the first nine months of 2026, and gave Fontaine's think tank $450,000.

paras.p1520: The trust alone chooses the Class T directors who form the board majority, while holders of ordinary Class A shares and founder Class F stock together elect the remaining directors.

s344.tldr: The trust alone chooses the Class T directors, who form the board majority. Holders of ordinary Class A shares and founder Class F stock together elect the remaining directors. Anyone nominating or removing a director must give the board's nominating and governance committee 30 days' notice unless it is waived. After the IPO, that committee will have one trust-elected director and two others. For one designated trust seat, the trust needs the committee's agreement to nominate, remove or change it, and disputes go to a vote of Class E shareholders. Removing that director for cause requires only 30 days' notice to the founders' entity and the committee.

paras.p1523: This introduces the conditions, called the Trust Amendment Threshold, under which the trust's rules and the rights of its Class T stock can be changed.
paras.p1524: If the trustees support a change, it needs approval from 80% of the board and 80% of the trustees.

paras.p1526: For three years after the IPO, a change without trustee support needs unanimous founder approval plus majority votes from Class E and Class A shareholders, each with minimum turnout requirements.
paras.p1527: At any time, a change without trustee support can also pass with two thirds of the founders, 75% of Class E votes cast, and a majority of Class A votes cast, each with turnout minimums.
paras.p1528: Once founder Class F stock no longer exists, changing the trust's terms against trustee wishes requires approval of 85% of all outstanding Class A shares, a very high bar.
paras.p1529: Using the same approval thresholds, Anthropic could also cancel the trust's Class T stock without paying for it, which would end the trust's power to pick directors.

s345.tldr: Anthropic could change the trust's rules and its Class T stock rights, or even cancel that stock without payment and end the trust's power to pick directors, if set approval thresholds are met. With trustee support, a change needs 80% of the board and 80% of the trustees. Without trustee support, while founder Class F stock exists, there are two routes. For three years after the IPO, a change needs unanimous founder approval plus majority Class E and Class A votes. At any time, it can pass with two thirds of the founders, 75% of Class E votes cast and a majority of Class A votes cast. Both routes have turnout minimums. Once Class F stock is gone, overriding the trustees requires 85% of all outstanding Class A shares.

paras.p1546: If fewer than three qualifying Continuing Founders remain for 90 straight days, a 450 day transition begins, after which the Class F and Class E stock is cancelled without payment and founder control ends.

paras.p1548: A founder leaves the founders' company upon resignation, death or incapacity, falling below 2% of their IPO-time Class A holdings, removal for cause including competing, a successor's ten year limit, or an approved leave of absence.

s348.tldr: Before the IPO, the seven co-founders' company will receive one Class F share carrying 50.1% of all shareholder votes, and new share issues will never dilute it. That means the founders will control votes on directors not chosen by the trust, charter changes and mergers or sales, limiting other shareholders' influence. The founders decide by majority, and a deadlock is cast in line with public Class A votes. Founders leave the group on resignation, death, removal for cause or holdings falling below 2% of their IPO level. If fewer than three remain for 90 days, a 450 day transition ends with founder and employee Class E stock cancelled without payment. The founders are Dario and Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish and Christopher Olah, each pledging 80% of equity to charity.

They are Dario Amodei, CEO; Daniela Amodei, President and board chair; Tom Brown, Chief Compute Officer, who manages chips and data centers and led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI; and Jack Clark, head of the Anthropic Institute, which shares research publicly, and a former OpenAI Policy Director. The others are Jared Kaplan, Chief Science Officer and co-author of the scaling laws on how AI improves with size, data and compute; Sam McCandlish, Chief Architect, whose OpenAI research helped enable GPT-3; and Christopher Olah, who leads research into how models work internally. Benjamin Mann, often called a co-founder, has no Class F vote.

paras.p1562: Class E shares, which go to employees, carry almost no voting power: they vote only on disputes over one specific trust-elected director and on changes to the Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT) or its special Class T shares.
paras.p1563: If the nominating committee and the trust disagree about the Specified Class T Director, employees holding Class E shares decide by simple majority, with at least half of all Class E shares taking part.
paras.p1564: Changing the trust's rules, its Class T shares' rights, or buying back those shares needs approval from public Class A holders and also from employee Class E holders, under the thresholds listed next.
paras.p1565: For three years after the IPO, if all continuing founders back such a change through their Class F shares, employees can approve it by simple majority with only 40% of Class E shares participating.
paras.p1566: Otherwise, while founder Class F shares exist, employees must approve trust changes by 75% of votes cast, a high bar that makes weakening the trust difficult.
paras.p1567: Employees will receive one Class E share per six months worked and one per Class A share pledged to charity through Anthropic's donation matching; co-founders get none, and timing will be set after the IPO.
paras.p1568: Class E shares are temporary: half are cancelled each year after an employee leaves, all are cancelled on death, firing for cause, or joining a direct competitor, and all disappear once founder shares are gone, with no payment.

s351.tldr: Class E shares, given to employees, carry almost no voting power. They vote only on disputes over one specific trust elected director and on changes to the Long-Term Benefit Trust or its Class T shares. Any change to the trust needs approval from both public Class A holders and Class E holders. For three years after the IPO, if all founders back a change, employees can approve it by simple majority with 40% participation; otherwise they need 75% of votes cast, a bar that makes weakening the trust hard. Employees earn one share per six months worked and per Class A share donated through matching; co-founders get none. The shares are temporary and are cancelled without payment after departure, on joining a competitor, or once founder shares end.

paras.p1570: The trust elects most of the board but does not run the company; its job is picking directors who balance shareholder profits, the interests of people affected by Anthropic, and the company's stated public benefit purpose.

s352.tldr: Under a new agreement, the trust and the founders' holding company will together choose every board member, and directors have no term limits. Because the founders' Class F share carries 50.1% of all shareholder votes, the founders will elect the directors the trust does not pick and decide every shareholder vote, including any merger or sale, for the foreseeable future. The trust elects most of the board but does not run the company; its role is to choose directors who balance profits, the people affected by Anthropic and its public benefit purpose. Nasdaq lets Anthropic skip some governance rules as a result, but Anthropic says it will use this only for a nominating committee that will not be fully independent.

paras.p1573: This table explains how Anthropic's two special control classes can end. Trust control (Class T) ends only if that stock is redeemed or eliminated with trustee-level approval. Founder control (Class F) ends if that stock disappears or fewer than three founders remain.
paras.p1574: When the trustees support ending their own class, 80% of Anthropic's board and 80% of the trustees must approve. The founder transition starts after fewer than three qualifying founders remain for 90 straight days, and founders can be removed from the founder group in several ways.

paras.p1577: If founder stock is gone and the trustees object, 85% of all Class A shares can end trust control. It never ends automatically or with time, and once ended it cannot be reversed. Removing a founder for incapacity or cause requires a formal determination the founder can contest.
paras.p1578: Before a founder can be removed for incapacity, cause or low ownership, a majority of the other founders must send written notice through the Founder LLC, the entity holding the founders' stock.
paras.p1579: If a founder dies or becomes incapacitated within ten years after the offering, a replacement can join and count toward the three founders needed to keep founder control, but only until that tenth anniversary.
paras.p1580: Once founder control ends, it cannot be extended, delayed or waived.
paras.p1581: Until trust control ends, the LTBT elects a board majority. Founder stock carries 50.1% of all votes, so if trust control ends first, the founders control every shareholder vote. Ordinary Class A shareholders gain full control only after both classes end.
paras.p1582: This points readers to the risk factors and capital stock description for more detail on Anthropic's governance structure.

s353.tldr: Class A shareholders gain full control of Anthropic after both special classes end. Until trust control (Class T) ends, the LTBT elects a board majority; founder stock (Class F) holds 50.1% of votes, so founders control every shareholder vote if trust control ends first. Irreversibly ending trust control needs 80% of board and trustees or, over trustee objection, founders, Class E and Class A holders, or 85% of Class A shares once founder stock is gone. Founder control ends permanently if fewer than three founders remain for 90 days. Founders leave by resigning, dying, competing, holding under 2% of original shares, or approved leave; replacements count only until the offering's tenth anniversary.

s416.tldr: Anthropic's new 2026 stock plan was approved by shareholders October 22, 2026 and starts just before the IPO. Its share pool, size left blank, can grow automatically by up to 5% of outstanding economic shares each year from 2027 through 2036, diluting other holders. The plan lets the compensation committee reprice options lower and caps outside director pay at $1,000,000 a year, or $2,000,000 in the first year. Awards can be cancelled for nothing in a sale and can be clawed back. The 2021 plan, which reserved 3,864,826,090 Class A shares, stops new awards, and its lapsed shares move to the new pool. A 2026 employee plan lets staff buy shares through payroll at up to a 15% discount, up to $25,000 a year. Its pool grows up to 1% yearly through 2036.

paras.p1750: Anthropic's new stock plan for paying employees in equity was adopted by the board on September 1, 2026, approved by shareholders on October 22, 2026, and starts just before the IPO registration takes effect.
paras.p1751: The 2026 plan's share pool combines a new allotment with shares left over or returned from the older 2021 plan, though the filing leaves the exact share counts blank.
paras.p1752: Each year from 2027 through 2036 the pool can grow automatically by up to 5% of Anthropic's outstanding economic common shares, or a smaller number the board chooses, which can steadily dilute other shareholders.
paras.p1753: Shares from awards that lapse, are forfeited, are held back to cover prices or taxes, or are paid out in cash go back into the pool for future grants rather than being used up.
paras.p1754: The board's compensation committee runs the plan and has wide power over who gets awards and on what terms, including the power to reprice options to a lower purchase price or swap them for other awards or cash.
paras.p1755: Employees, outside directors and consultants, including workers hired through staffing agencies, can receive awards under the plan.
paras.p1756: The plan can grant several kinds of equity: stock options, stock appreciation rights, restricted stock, restricted stock units and stock bonuses.
paras.p1757: Options generally must let holders buy shares at no less than the market value on the grant date and last at most 10 years, with stricter limits for tax favored options held by anyone owning over 10% of the voting power.
paras.p1758: The committee sets how options are paid for and when they vest, and departing holders can generally use vested options for a set period, never beyond the option's term.
paras.p1759: Stock appreciation rights pay the rise in Anthropic's share price after the grant date, in cash or shares, with a starting price no lower than the market value at grant.
paras.p1760: Restricted stock gives actual shares up front that cannot be sold and can be taken back until conditions are met, and holders usually get voting and dividend rights immediately.
paras.p1761: A restricted stock unit is a promise of one share's value, paid in stock or cash once conditions set by the committee are met, possibly with payments matching any dividends.
paras.p1762: Stock bonus awards hand over shares for no purchase price, paid in stock or cash as the committee decides.
paras.p1763: Each outside director's yearly stock awards plus board fees are capped at $1,000,000, or $2,000,000 in the first year of service, limiting how much Anthropic can pay non-employee directors.
paras.p1764: Awards generally cannot be transferred except through inheritance, and only the recipient can exercise options during their lifetime.
paras.p1765: If Anthropic splits its stock, merges or makes similar changes to its shares, the committee adjusts awards so they are neither diluted nor inflated by the event.
paras.p1766: If Anthropic is wound up or liquidated, participants get notice and any awards not already exercised or paid out are cancelled.
paras.p1767: In a sale of the company or of most of its assets, the committee can, without employees' consent, continue, convert, cash out, speed up or even cancel awards for nothing.
paras.p1768: Individual award agreements can promise extra early vesting if Anthropic undergoes a change in control.
paras.p1769: A change in control means a merger, asset sale, takeover of 50% voting power, or replacement of most directors within 12 months, but the board replacement test only applies after both the Class F and Class T Sunset Times defined in the new charter.
paras.p1770: Awards can be reduced or clawed back under any compensation recovery policy in force or adopted to comply with law.
paras.p1771: The committee can change or end the plan without harming existing awards unless agreed, tax favored options stop after 10 years, and shareholder approval is sought where law or exchange rules require.

s417.tldr: Anthropic's new 2026 stock plan for paying staff in equity was adopted by the board September 1, 2026, approved by shareholders October 22, 2026, and starts just before the IPO. The share pool, left blank in the filing, includes leftover 2021 plan shares. It can grow automatically by up to 5% of outstanding economic shares each year from 2027 through 2036, diluting other holders, and lapsed or withheld shares return to it. Employees, outside directors and consultants can receive options, stock appreciation rights, restricted stock, RSUs and stock bonuses. The compensation committee can reprice options lower. Outside director pay is capped at $1,000,000 a year, $2,000,000 in the first year. In a sale, awards can be cancelled for nothing without consent, and awards can be clawed back.

paras.p1772: The older 2021 plan, adopted January 28, 2021 and last amended effective May 28, 2026, stops issuing new awards before the IPO, though existing awards keep their original terms.
paras.p1773: The 2021 plan reserved 3,864,826,090 Class A shares, and shares from its lapsed, forfeited or withheld awards will flow into the new 2026 plan's pool.
paras.p1774: The board ran the 2021 plan before the IPO and hands that role to the compensation committee afterward.
paras.p1775: Under the 2021 plan Anthropic has already granted stock options, restricted stock and restricted stock units.
paras.p1776: As with the new plan, 2021 plan awards generally pass only by inheritance and only the holder can exercise options while alive.
paras.p1777: The committee adjusts 2021 plan awards after stock splits or similar capital changes so their value is not unfairly shrunk or enlarged.
paras.p1778: In a sale or takeover, the committee can, without consent, keep, convert, cash out or cancel for nothing the awards granted under the 2021 plan.
paras.p1779: The board can amend or end the 2021 plan, seeking shareholder approval where needed, but no new awards will be made under it after the offering.

s418.tldr: Anthropic's older 2021 stock plan was adopted January 28, 2021 and last amended effective May 28, 2026. It stops issuing new awards before the IPO, though existing awards keep their terms. The plan reserved 3,864,826,090 Class A shares and has already granted options, restricted stock and restricted stock units. Shares from its lapsed, forfeited or withheld awards will move into the 2026 plan's pool. The board ran the plan before the IPO, and the compensation committee takes over afterward. Awards pass only by inheritance and are adjusted after stock splits. In a sale or takeover, awards can be kept, converted, cashed out or cancelled for nothing without consent.

paras.p1780: Anthropic's employee stock purchase plan lets staff buy company shares through payroll. The board adopted it on September 1, 2026, stockholders approved it on October 22, 2026, and it takes effect just before the IPO registration does.
paras.p1781: The plan has one part designed to meet Section 423 of the tax code, which gives employees favorable tax treatment, and a second part for purchase rights that do not meet those rules.
paras.p1782: This draft of the filing leaves blank the maximum number of Class A shares the plan can issue.
paras.p1783: Each year from fiscal 2027 through fiscal 2036, the plan's share pool can grow automatically by up to 1% of outstanding economic common stock, or less if the board decides, which gradually dilutes other shareholders.
paras.p1784: The board has handed the running of the plan to its compensation committee.
paras.p1785: Most regular employees, including executives, can join the plan. So can certain service providers of Anthropic and its designated affiliates, including those outside the United States.
paras.p1786: For the tax-favored part, Anthropic may require things like two years of service or more than 20 hours a week. Each employee is capped at $25,000 of stock per year, and anyone holding 5% or more is excluded.
paras.p1787: Employees buy shares in offering periods of up to 27 months with set purchase dates. If the share price falls to or below the starting price, that offering can end and employees move into a new one.
paras.p1788: Employees pay through payroll deductions, capped at 15% of earnings in the tax-favored part. In the other part, contributions are generally made after tax, as the administrator decides.
paras.p1789: Employees pay no less than 85% of the lower of two prices: the share price when the offering starts or the price on the purchase date. That is a discount of up to 15% off the lower price.
paras.p1790: If Anthropic splits its stock, merges, pays stock dividends or otherwise restructures its shares, the board will proportionally adjust the plan's share limits, annual increases and purchase prices.
paras.p1791: If Anthropic dissolves or liquidates, any offering under way ends early. Employees' rights are used to buy shares automatically before the wind-down unless they withdraw first.
paras.p1792: If Anthropic is sold, merged, or someone gains over 50% of its stock, the buyer may take over employees' purchase rights. If it does not, employees' saved contributions buy shares before the deal closes.
paras.p1793: In a spin off, the board may adjust ongoing offerings. Otherwise, employees of a unit that leaves the group are treated as if they had left Anthropic.
paras.p1794: The board can change or end the plan at any time but generally cannot materially harm existing purchase rights. It will seek stockholder approval where law or stock exchange rules require it.

s419.tldr: Anthropic's 2026 employee stock purchase plan lets staff buy shares through payroll at up to a 15% discount off the lower of the price when an offering starts or on the purchase date. The board adopted it September 1, 2026, stockholders approved it October 22, 2026, and it starts just before the IPO. The maximum share count is left blank. The pool can grow by up to 1% of outstanding economic stock yearly from fiscal 2027 through 2036, diluting other holders. Most employees, including executives and some non US service providers, can join. The tax favored part caps payroll deductions at 15% of earnings and purchases at $25,000 a year, and excludes 5% holders. Offerings last up to 27 months.

paras.p1826: The new charter, effective just before the IPO, shields directors and certain officers from personal money damages for breaching their duties, as far as Delaware corporate law (the DGCL) allows, except in the cases listed below.

paras.p1837: Some outside directors may also be insured or protected through their own employers.

s440.tldr: The new charter, effective just before the IPO, shields directors and certain officers from personal money damages for breaching their duties as far as Delaware law allows, and further if that law loosens. The exceptions are disloyalty, bad faith, intentional misconduct, knowingly breaking the law, improper personal benefit and, for directors, illegal dividends or buybacks. Officers stay liable to the company itself. Bylaws, individual agreements and insurance make Anthropic cover leaders' liabilities and advance their legal costs, and the IPO banks will cover certain liabilities. This may discourage shareholder suits and cost shareholders money. Failing to balance public benefit against stockholder interests does not remove protection unless there is a conflict. The SEC considers indemnification for securities law liabilities unenforceable.

s444.tldr: The new charter authorizes 460,000,000,002 shares. These are up to 300,000,000,000 voting Class A shares sold to the public, 100,000,000,000 nonvoting Class N, 30,000,000,000 employee Class E and 30,000,000,000 preferred, none outstanding. There is also one Class T share for the Long-Term Benefit Trust and one Class F share for the founders' LLC. Class F carries a fixed 50.1% of all voting power, and Class T elects a board majority. Class A has one vote per share, Classes T and E vote on limited matters, and Class N has no vote. Only Classes A and N get dividends and liquidation proceeds, and Anthropic cannot buy them back. Anthropic can cancel Class T, F and E shares for nothing when certain events occur. Outstanding counts are blank.

paras.p1871: Anthropic has four kinds of common stock, listed below.
paras.p1872: The economic shares, called Participating Common Stock, come in two series: voting Class A and nonvoting Class N.

s445.tldr: The founders' single Class F share carries 50.1% of voting power on ordinary matters, including director elections. The Long-Term Benefit Trust's Class T share elects a board majority. Ordinary Class A shareholders, with one vote per share, control Anthropic only after both structures end. The trust share never ends automatically. Cancelling it needs 80% of the board and trustees, or founder, employee Class E and Class A approval if trustees object, or 85% of Class A shares once the founder share is gone. Founder control ends after fewer than three Continuing Founders remain for 90 days. Nonvoting Class N, held mainly by strategic partners, becomes Class A when sold publicly. Only Classes A and N get dividends or liquidation proceeds, and the special classes receive $0.00001 per share.

paras.p1877: Class N shareholders cannot vote except where Delaware law requires it, such as charter changes that would hurt Class N specifically.

paras.p1880: Employee Class E shares vote only on limited issues: one trust appointed director if the board's nominating committee disagrees, changes to the trust or its share, and getting rid of the trust share.

s446.tldr: The founders' single Class F share always carries 50.1% of total voting power on ordinary matters, including director elections, and is voted as the founders' LLC decides. Class A shareholders get one vote per share on ordinary matters, including electing the directors the trust does not choose. The trust's Class T share does not vote on ordinary matters. It elects a majority of the board and votes on removing employee Class E shares and on changes to founder rights. Class N shareholders vote only where Delaware law requires it. Employee Class E shares vote only on limited trust related issues.

paras.p1882: Class N shares are held mainly by strategic business partners and become voting Class A when sold publicly or to an unrelated buyer who will own no more than 9.99% of any class.

paras.p1885: Employee Class E shares cannot be converted or transferred.

s447.tldr: Class A shares can be sold freely, subject to the law and to lockup periods after the IPO that restrict selling for a time. Class N shares are held mainly by strategic business partners. They become voting Class A shares when sold publicly or to an unrelated buyer who will own no more than 9.99% of any class. The trust's Class T share can be transferred only with approval from the group that can change or end the trust. The founder Class F share moves only in a board approved reorganization of the LLC that keeps the same members. Employee Class E shares cannot be converted or transferred.

paras.p1886: Neither Anthropic nor holders can force a buyback of Class A shares.
paras.p1887: Neither Anthropic nor holders can force a buyback of Class N shares.
paras.p1888: The trust's Class T share can be cancelled for nothing under the conditions below, which is how the trust's board control could be removed.
paras.p1889: If the trustees agree, cancellation needs approval from 80% of board seats and 80% of trustees.
paras.p1890: If the founder share still exists and the trustees oppose, either of the following two paths applies.

paras.p1893: If the founder share no longer exists and the trustees oppose, removing the trust share requires 85% of all outstanding Class A shares, a very high bar.
paras.p1894: The founder share can be cancelled for nothing by a supermajority of remaining founders, if the LLC dissolves, or after fewer than three founders remain for 90 consecutive days.
paras.p1895: Departing employees lose half their Class E shares each year and lose all of them on death, incapacity, firing for cause or joining a direct competitor; all Class E shares vanish if the founder share ends or with board, founder and trust approval.

s448.tldr: No one can force a buyback of Class A or Class N shares. The trust's Class T share, which gives the trust its board control, can be cancelled for nothing. With trustee agreement, cancellation needs 80% of board seats and 80% of trustees. If the trustees oppose and the founder share exists, it needs founder approval plus approval from employee Class E and Class A holders. Until the IPO's third anniversary, founder approval must be unanimous. If the founder share is gone, it needs 85% of all Class A shares. The founder share ends by founder supermajority, LLC dissolution, or fewer than three founders for 90 days. Departing employees lose their Class E shares over time or at once.

paras.p1896: Only Class A and Class N shareholders can receive dividends, and only when the board chooses; the trust, founder and employee classes never receive dividends.

s449.tldr: Only Class A and Class N shareholders can receive dividends, and only when the board chooses; the trust, founder and employee classes never receive dividends.

paras.p1900: Two control features can end permanently: the Long Term Benefit Trust's Class T stock ends only through redemption or amendment with the Trust Amendment Threshold's approval, and the founders' Class F stock ends once fewer than three Continuing Founders remain for 90 consecutive days.
paras.p1901: If the Trustees support ending Class T stock, 80% of the board and 80% of the Trustees must approve; non qualifying successor members do not count toward the three founders needed to keep Class F control.
paras.p1902: Without Trustee support, ending Class T stock needs founder, Class E and Class A approvals, with stricter terms until the third anniversary of the offering; founders lose their seat on resignation, death, incapacity, cause, leave, or falling below 2% of their shares.
paras.p1903: This is only a repeated table header for the Class T and Class F sunset comparison.

paras.p1906: During the first ten years after the offering, a founder who dies or becomes incapacitated can be replaced by a successor who counts toward the three founders needed, but only until the tenth anniversary.
paras.p1907: Once the founders' Class F control ends, it is permanent and cannot be extended, delayed or waived.
paras.p1908: While both exist, the Trust elects a board majority and the Founder LLC holds 50.1% of stockholder votes; if one structure ends the other keeps its power, and only after both end do ordinary Class A shareholders control.

s453.tldr: While both control structures exist, the Long Term Benefit Trust elects a board majority and the Founder LLC holds 50.1% of stockholder votes. If one ends, the other keeps its power, and only after both end do ordinary Class A shareholders control Anthropic. The trust's Class T stock ends only by redemption or approved amendment, never automatically. Without founder or trustee support, ending it requires 85% of Class A shares. The founders' Class F control ends permanently once fewer than three Continuing Founders remain for 90 consecutive days. Founders lose their status through resignation, death, incapacity, cause, leave or falling below 2% of their shares. For ten years after the offering, successors can replace founders who die or become incapacitated.

s457.tldr: Some existing investors, plus Google and Broadcom under separate agreements, can make Anthropic register their shares for public sale at its expense, subject to lockups. paras.p1918: Delaware law and Anthropic's charter and bylaws contain features that make takeovers harder, which Anthropic says push acquirers to negotiate with the board and may produce better terms.

s463.tldr: Anthropic's charter and bylaws make hostile takeovers hard. The trust and the Founder LLC together elect the whole board, and the Founder LLC decides shareholder votes, including on a sale, so Class A holders generally cannot change outcomes. Only the trust fills trust seats, and changing board size needs 80% board approval. Once founder control ends, directors serve staggered three year terms. Other holders face strict notice rules, cannot call special meetings or pool votes, and amendments need 66 2/3% of Class A votes. Anthropic can issue up to 30,000,000,000 preferred shares with custom rights. Most shareholder suits must go to Delaware or federal courts. Delaware's limits on deals with 15% holders apply only after both control structures end. Anthropic says all this pushes buyers to negotiate.

paras.p1919: Anthropic opts out of Delaware's Section 203 until both the Class T and Class F structures end, after which it cannot do major deals with a new large holder for three years unless one condition below applies:
paras.p1920: The first exception is that the board approved the deal before the buyer became a large holder.
paras.p1921: The second exception is that the buyer ended up owning at least 85% of the voting stock in that transaction, excluding certain insider and employee plan shares.
paras.p1922: The third exception is board approval plus a meeting vote of two thirds of the voting stock the buyer does not own.
paras.p1923: Section 203 targets mergers, asset sales and similar deals with anyone owning, or recently owning, 15% or more of the voting power.

s464.tldr: Anthropic opts out of Delaware's Section 203 until both the trust and founder control structures end. That law limits mergers, asset sales and similar deals with anyone owning, or recently owning, 15% or more of the voting power. Once it applies, such a deal is barred for three years unless one of three conditions is met. The board approved the deal before the buyer became a large holder, or the buyer reached 85% of voting stock in that transaction, or the board and two thirds of the other voting stock approve.

paras.p1924: This introduces charter and bylaw features that could deter hostile takeovers or delay changes in the board or management.

s465.tldr: Anthropic's charter and bylaws could deter hostile takeovers. The trust and the Founder LLC will together elect the whole board, and the Founder LLC decides shareholder votes, including on a sale. Class A holders therefore generally cannot change outcomes. Only the trust fills trust seats, and changing board size needs 80% board approval. Once founder control ends, directors serve staggered three year terms. Other shareholders face strict advance notice rules, cannot call special meetings, cannot pool votes on one candidate, and have limited written consent rights. Amendments later need 66 2/3% of Class A votes. Anthropic can issue up to 30,000,000,000 preferred shares with custom rights. Most shareholder suits must be filed in Delaware or federal courts.

paras.p1925: The Trust and the Founder LLC will together elect the whole board, and the Founder LLC will decide shareholder votes, including on a sale, so Class A holders generally cannot change outcomes unless the founders deadlock.

s468.tldr: Only the Trust fills Trust director vacancies, the Founder LLC effectively steers other vacancies, and changing board size needs 80% board approval, keeping outsiders from enlarging the board to seize control.

s469.tldr: Shareholders other than the Trust and Founder LLC must follow strict advance notice rules to propose business or nominate directors, and the board's nominating committee gets 30 days' notice of Trust and Founder LLC director changes.

s488.tldr: Foreign investors generally face a 30% U.S. withholding tax on Class A dividends unless a tax treaty sets a lower rate, claimed on an IRS Form W-8. Gains on a sale are usually untaxed, with three exceptions. Gains tied to a U.S. business are taxed. So are gains of individuals present in the United States 183 days or more. A third exception would apply if Anthropic held mostly U.S. real estate, which it believes it does not. Backup withholding of 24% can apply without proof of foreign status. FATCA allows 30% withholding on dividends to foreign entities that do not report their U.S. owners. The summary excludes many special investors, rests on law that could change, and is not tax advice.

paras.p2009: A non-U.S. holder is an owner of Class A shares who is neither a partnership nor one of the U.S. taxpayers listed next.

paras.p2011: Corporations organized in the United States are not non-U.S. holders.
paras.p2012: Estates whose income is fully taxed by the United States are not non-U.S. holders.
paras.p2013: Trusts supervised by a U.S. court and controlled by U.S. persons, or that elected U.S. treatment, are not non-U.S. holders.

s489.tldr: For tax purposes, a non-U.S. holder is an owner of Class A shares who is not a partnership and not a U.S. taxpayer. U.S. taxpayers here are U.S. citizens and residents, corporations organized in the United States, estates whose income is fully taxed by the United States, and trusts that are supervised by a U.S. court and controlled by U.S. persons or that elected U.S. treatment.

paras.p2014: Payments to shareholders count as taxable dividends only to the extent of Anthropic's tax-measured profits; anything beyond that first lowers the investor's cost basis and then counts as gain on a sale.
paras.p2015: Foreign investors generally face a 30% U.S. withholding tax on dividends unless a tax treaty sets a lower rate, and any excess withheld can be reclaimed from the IRS.
paras.p2016: To get a lower treaty rate, a foreign investor must give the withholding agent the correct IRS Form W-8 with a taxpayer number and keep it current, often passing it through their broker.
paras.p2017: Dividends tied to a foreign investor's U.S. business avoid withholding with Form W-8ECI but are taxed at normal U.S. rates, and foreign companies may also owe a 30% branch profits tax.

s490.tldr: Foreign investors generally face a 30% U.S. withholding tax on dividends unless a tax treaty sets a lower rate, and any excess withheld can be reclaimed from the IRS. Payments count as taxable dividends only up to Anthropic's profits as measured for tax; anything beyond that first lowers the investor's cost basis and then counts as gain on a sale. To get a treaty rate, the investor must give the correct IRS Form W-8, with a taxpayer number, and keep it current, often through a broker. Dividends tied to a U.S. business avoid withholding with Form W-8ECI but are taxed at normal U.S. rates, and foreign companies may also owe a 30% branch profits tax.

paras.p2018: Foreign investors generally owe no U.S. tax on gains from selling Class A shares, except in the three situations listed next.
paras.p2019: The first exception is when the gain is tied to the investor's U.S. trade or business.
paras.p2020: The second exception is for a foreign individual present in the United States 183 days or more in the year of the sale, if other conditions are met.
paras.p2021: The third exception applies if Anthropic is treated as a company holding mostly U.S. real estate and the investor owned more than 5% of the publicly traded Class A shares during the relevant period.
paras.p2022: A company counts as a U.S. real property holding corporation if U.S. real estate is at least half its assets; Anthropic believes it is not one and will not become one, but cannot guarantee it.
paras.p2023: Business-connected gains are taxed at regular U.S. rates, plus a possible 30% branch profits tax for companies, while gains of individuals present 183 days face a 30% tax that U.S. capital losses can offset.

s491.tldr: Foreign investors generally owe no U.S. tax on gains from selling Class A shares, with three exceptions. The first is gains tied to the investor's U.S. business, which are taxed at regular rates, plus a possible 30% branch profits tax for companies. The second is foreign individuals present in the United States 183 days or more in the year of sale, who face a 30% tax that U.S. capital losses can offset. The third applies if Anthropic is a U.S. real property holding corporation, meaning U.S. real estate is at least half its assets, and the investor owned more than 5% of the traded shares. Anthropic believes it is not one and will not become one, but cannot guarantee it.

paras.p2024: Anthropic must report dividends paid and tax withheld to the IRS each year, send a copy to the investor, and the IRS may share it with the investor's home country.
paras.p2025: Dividends and sale proceeds may face reporting and a 24% backup withholding unless the investor proves foreign status on the proper IRS Form W-8.
paras.p2026: Sales through a U.S. broker office face reporting and backup withholding unless foreign status is certified; sales through foreign brokers usually do not, except brokers with major U.S. ties or when the payer knows the holder is American.
paras.p2027: Backup withholding is not an extra tax; it counts toward the investor's U.S. tax bill and any overpayment can be refunded if the IRS gets the information on time.

s492.tldr: Anthropic must report dividends paid and tax withheld to the IRS each year and send the investor a copy, and the IRS may share it with the investor's home country. Dividends and sale proceeds may face reporting and 24% backup withholding unless the investor proves foreign status on an IRS Form W-8. Sales through a U.S. broker office are covered unless foreign status is certified. Sales through foreign brokers usually are not, except for brokers with major U.S. ties or when the payer knows the holder is American. Backup withholding is not an extra tax: it counts toward the investor's U.S. tax bill, and overpayments can be refunded if the IRS gets the information on time.

s531.tldr: Grant Thornton, for 2023 and 2024, and Ernst & Young, for 2025, gave clean audit opinions, though neither audited internal controls. Ernst & Young named note valuation and lawsuits as its hardest judgments. Revenue reached $16.286B in the first half of 2026, but the net loss was $80.748B. Cloud marketplaces brought 48% of revenue. Noncancelable infrastructure commitments reached about $265.6B, and about $245B more has been signed since. About $23.7B of stock unit cost is not yet recorded.

s534.tldr: Ernst & Young flagged two areas of its 2025 audit that required its hardest judgments, without changing its clean opinion. The bigger one is convertible notes, loans that can turn into shares and are carried at market value. They were worth $41.7B at December 31, 2025, producing a $34.5B loss for 2025, and their value swings sharply with judgments such as how likely an IPO was and how two valuation methods are weighted. In an IPO they automatically become nonvoting Class N shares at $2.0928 (2023 notes) or $5.0478 (2024 notes), or the IPO price if lower. A cap on Amazon's ownership, which Amazon can waive, limits conversion, and blocked amounts are reissued as interest free notes. s611.tldr: In 2023 Anthropic raised $122 million through SAFEs, agreements where investors pay now and receive shares in a later funding round, sometimes at a discount. $1 million became Series C-1 shares in 2023 and $121 million became Series D shares in 2024. Because they promised a fixed dollar value in a varying number of shares, the accounting rules required Anthropic to treat them as liabilities revalued at market value. None have been outstanding since the end of 2024.

paras.p2438: None of the value changes through June 30, 2026 came from shifts in how likely Anthropic was to repay its debts.

None of the value changes through June 30, 2026 came from shifts in Anthropic's own credit risk.

paras.p2603: Delaware corporate law allows a company to cover the legal costs and liabilities of its officers and directors, which is the basis for the protections described next.
paras.p2604: Anthropic's new charter, effective just before the IPO, will shield directors and certain officers from personal money damages for breaching their duties to the company, with the exceptions listed next.
paras.p2605: The first exception is that directors and officers remain liable if they are disloyal to Anthropic or its stockholders.
paras.p2606: They also remain liable for acting in bad faith, intentional misconduct or knowingly breaking the law.
paras.p2607: Directors remain liable for paying dividends or buying back stock in ways Delaware law prohibits.
paras.p2608: They remain liable for any deal from which they improperly gained a personal benefit.
paras.p2609: Officers, unlike directors, are not shielded from claims brought by or on behalf of Anthropic itself.
paras.p2610: Later changes to these protections will not remove coverage for past conduct, and if Delaware law loosens liability further, Anthropic's leaders automatically get the broader protection.
paras.p2611: Anthropic's new bylaws will require it to cover legal claims and advance legal costs for current and former directors and officers, and allow it to do the same for employees and agents.
paras.p2612: Anthropic has signed or will sign separate agreements with each director and executive officer that may protect them more broadly than Delaware law, saying this is needed to attract and keep qualified leaders.
paras.p2613: These protections may discourage shareholder lawsuits against leaders and cost shareholders if Anthropic pays settlements; no such claims are known now, and failing to balance public benefit goals alone does not count as bad faith or disloyalty.
paras.p2614: Anthropic has bought insurance that covers its directors and executive officers for claims of wrongdoing, including securities claims, and reimburses Anthropic for amounts it pays to protect them.
paras.p2615: Some outside directors may also be protected through their own employers against liabilities from serving on Anthropic's board.
paras.p2616: The underwriting banks will agree to cover Anthropic and its leaders for certain legal liabilities connected to the offering.

s653.tldr: Under Delaware law, Anthropic's new charter, effective just before the IPO, will shield directors and certain officers from personal money damages for breaching their duties. Exceptions cover disloyalty, bad faith, intentional misconduct, knowing lawbreaking, improper dividends or buybacks, and improper personal benefit. Officers are not shielded from claims by Anthropic itself. Bylaws and individual agreements require Anthropic to cover leaders' legal claims and costs. Anthropic says this helps attract leaders, but it may discourage shareholder suits and cost shareholders. No such claims are known. Failing to balance public benefit goals alone is not bad faith. Insurance, some directors' employers and the underwriters provide further coverage.

Each later amendment with a prospectus will be treated as a fresh registration for liability purposes.

s663.tldr: The exhibits include Anthropic's current and post IPO charters and bylaws. They also include partly redacted 2026 funding agreements with Amazon Web Services, Google and Broadcom, the employee stock plans, the director pay policy and the Donation Matching Plan. Other exhibits are office leases, the September 4, 2026 credit agreement led by Morgan Stanley and a Broadcom equipment lease. Two agreements give the CEO voting power over shares held by charitable funds. The stockholders', trust and Founder LLC agreements, the auditor change letter and the auditor consents are attached. The underwriting agreement and the legal opinion will be filed later, and some confidential terms are removed.
